exact: Yes, genuinely — it's become the thing I look forward to most in a week, though I'd never have said that about myself five years ago. Back then I thought of walking as what you did when there was no better way of getting somewhere.

The reason it took hold is that it's the only exercise I've found where my mind actually goes quiet. In a gym I'm counting, checking the clock, thinking about the email I haven't answered. On a hill you have to watch where your feet land, and that small demand seems to crowd everything else out. There's also the fact that it's the one activity where being slow isn't failing at it.

The trip that turned it from an occasional thing into a habit was last autumn. A friend and I climbed a hill about an hour from my parents' house — nothing dramatic, maybe four hundred metres — and we set off at seven to catch the light. What I remember is that we barely spoke for three hours. Not because anything was wrong; there just wasn't anything that needed saying. We ate at the top, walked down, and I got home at two in the afternoon feeling like I'd been away for a week. I've gone back to the same hill probably nine or ten times since.

So if you asked me what hiking gives me, I wouldn't say fitness, even though that's a side effect. It's more that it's the only reliable way I've found to put a gap between me and my own head, and at this point I'd protect that time over almost anything else in my week.
喜欢，是真的喜欢——现在它是我一周里最期待的事。不过五年前的我大概不会这么说，那时候我觉得走路只是没有更好的交通方式时才做的事。
它之所以能变成习惯，主要是因为这是我找到的唯一一种能让脑子真正安静下来的运动。在健身房我会一直数数、看时间、想那封还没回的邮件；但在山上你必须盯着脚下的路，这个小小的要求好像就把别的都挤出去了。还有一点是，这是少数几件“慢”不算失败的事。
让它从偶尔为之变成习惯的，是去年秋天那一次。我和一个朋友爬了我父母家附近的一座山，离得大概一个小时车程，山不高，四百米左右，我们七点就出发，为的是赶上早上的光线。我印象最深的是，那三个小时我们几乎没说话——不是因为有什么问题，只是当时确实没有非说不可的事。我们在山顶吃了点东西，走下来，下午两点到家，感觉像是出去了一个星期。那之后我又去了同一座山，大概九到十次。
所以如果你问我徒步给了我什么，我不会说是身体变好，虽然那确实是副产品。更准确地说，它是我找到的唯一一种可靠的方式，能在我和我自己的脑子之间拉开一点距离。到现在，我会优先保住这段时间，几乎胜过我一周里的任何安排。

I've got two that have actually survived more than a year — cooking, and long walks with no destination. I've started plenty of others and quietly dropped them, so I've stopped counting anything as a hobby until it's lasted a full winter.

What those two have in common is that an evening spent on either of them leaves something behind. Office work rarely does — I can put in nine hours and struggle to name what changed. A meal exists and then gets eaten, which is a very short life, but at least somebody sat down to it. A walk gives me a route I now know. I think I need that more than I need the activity itself.

The clearest example is a soup my grandmother used to make. I'd asked her about it twice and both times got a version with no measurements in it — a handful of this, cook it until it looks right. Last month I finally worked it out by making it badly four times in a row and adjusting. The fourth one tasted like hers. I called my mother and she said it smelled like the right thing down the phone, which is obviously not possible, but I knew what she meant. I've made it four more times since, and I've written the recipe down properly for the first time in the family.

So when people ask what my hobbies are, the honest answer is that they're whatever produces evidence that the evening happened. That's why cooking and walking stuck and the others didn't — not because they're more interesting, but because they leave a mark.
有两个是真的坚持了一年以上的——做饭，还有那种没有目的地的长时间散步。别的我也开始过不少，但都悄悄放弃了，所以现在我不会把一件事算作爱好，除非它撑过了一个冬天。
这两件事的共同点是，一个晚上花在上面，结束之后都能留下点什么。办公室的工作很少有这种感觉，我可以干九个小时，却说不出到底改变了什么。一顿饭做出来又被吃掉，寿命当然很短，但至少有人坐下来吃了它。一次散步给我留下一条我现在认识的路线。我觉得比起活动本身，我更需要的是这个。
最清楚的例子是我奶奶以前常做的一道汤。我问过她两次，两次得到的说法里都没有分量——这个抓一把，煮到看起来差不多就行。上个月我终于做出来了，方法是连着做砸四次，每次调一点。第四次的味道和她做的一样。我给我妈打电话，她说隔着电话都闻得到那个味道，这当然不可能，但我明白她的意思。从那以后我又做了四次，而且我第一次把这个方子认真写了下来，我们家以前没人写过。
所以别人问我有什么爱好，老实的回答是：能留下证据、证明那个晚上确实存在过的事。这就是为什么做饭和散步留了下来，而别的没有——不是因为它们更有意思，而是因为它们会留下痕迹。

Japan, and I don't have to think about it, which is unusual for me — I'm normally the person who says it depends. But if someone gave me a ticket tomorrow and let me choose, I wouldn't hesitate at all.

What got me wasn't any of the things I'd been told to expect. It was how much care goes into things nobody would notice if it were absent. A train platform is clean in a way that implies somebody decided it should be. A bowl of noodles in a station is properly made. I found that genuinely moving after a while, because it suggests a shared idea that doing ordinary work badly is not acceptable, and that idea is much rarer than good scenery.

I was there nine days, two years ago, and the thing I still think about wasn't a temple. It was a restaurant in Kyoto with six seats and one dish on the menu. The man running it had been making the same thing for something like thirty years. There was no music, no decoration to speak of, and the meal took about twenty-five minutes. He watched us eat — not in an uncomfortable way, more the way you'd watch somebody open a present. I've eaten in far more impressive places and I can't tell you what was on the plate at any of them.

So my answer is Japan, but the reason isn't really about Japan. It's that going there changed what I notice when I travel anywhere. I used to look for the famous things; now the first thing I look at is how well the boring parts are done.
日本，而且我几乎不用想，这对我来说不常见——我平时是那种什么都要说“看情况”的人。但如果明天有人给我一张机票让我选，我完全不会犹豫。
打动我的并不是别人事先告诉我的那些东西，而是那些“做不好也没人会注意”的地方，居然被认真对待了。车站的月台干净得让人觉得，这是有人决定它应该这样。车站里一碗面也是好好做出来的。待久了我真的有点被这一点触动，因为它意味着大家有一个共同的想法：把普通的工作做差是不能接受的。而这种想法比好风景稀有得多。
我两年前在那边待了九天，到现在还常想起的不是什么寺庙，而是京都一家只有六个座位、菜单上只有一道菜的小店。做菜的人做同一样东西大概做了三十年。店里没有音乐，也谈不上什么装修，一顿饭大概二十五分钟。他会看着我们吃——不是那种让人不自在的看，更像是看别人拆礼物。我在比那气派得多的地方吃过饭，但一个盘子里有什么我都说不上来。
所以我的答案是日本，但理由其实不完全关于日本。而是去过那里以后，我在任何地方旅行时注意的东西都变了。我以前找的是有名的东西，现在我先看的是那些无聊的部分做得好不好。

Some of it, but not as a rule, and I've stopped feeling defensive about the inconsistency. I used to either buy everything organic for a month or nothing at all, and neither of those was a decision so much as a mood.

The reason I'm selective is that the price gap isn't the same size everywhere, and neither is the benefit. For some things I can taste the difference immediately and the premium is small. For others I'm paying forty percent more for something I genuinely cannot distinguish in a blind test, and I'd rather put that money into eating better in some other way — buying fish more often, say, or not letting vegetables go off in the drawer.

In practice that means eggs and leafy vegetables are always organic in my house, because with eggs the difference is visible before you've even cooked them, and greens go limp much faster if they've been treated to last. Rice, flour, tinned tomatoes — I buy whatever is there. I did try going fully organic for about six weeks two years ago and the honest outcome was that my shopping bill went up by roughly a third and I threw away more food, because I was buying carefully and then not cooking it.

So my position is that it's a series of small decisions rather than one big one. I think people get talked into treating it as an identity, and the version that actually survives contact with a weekly budget is much duller than that.
有些会买，但不是每次都买。我以前会一整个月什么都买有机的，或者干脆一样都不买，现在不会再为这种不一致感到心虚了——那两种做法与其说是决定，不如说是情绪。
我挑着买的原因是，差价不是每样东西都一样大，好处也不是。有些东西我一入口就能尝出区别，而且贵不了多少；有些东西我要多付四成的钱，买的却是我在盲测里根本分不出来的东西。那笔钱我宁愿用在别的地方把饭吃得更好，比如多买几次鱼，或者别让蔬菜烂在抽屉里。
具体来说，我家的鸡蛋和叶菜一定是有机的，因为鸡蛋的区别在下锅之前就看得出来，而叶菜如果做过处理，放久了反而蔫得更快。米、面粉、罐头番茄，有什么我就买什么。两年前我确实试过六个星期全买有机的，老实说结果是买菜的开销涨了大概三分之一，而且我扔掉的食物更多了，因为我买得很讲究，然后没做。
所以我的立场是：这是一连串的小决定，而不是一个大决定。我觉得很多人被说服把它当成一种身份，而真正能在每周的预算面前活下来的那个版本，要平淡得多。

Honestly, no — at least not in front of anyone. In an empty kitchen I'm perfectly happy, but the moment there's an audience something in me switches off, and I've made my peace with that rather than trying to fix it.

The reason is fairly simple: I can't stop watching myself do it. With most things I enjoy, I disappear into them and forget I'm being observed. Dancing does the opposite — the whole time I'm running a commentary on what my arms are doing, and that commentary is never generous. I know the standard advice is that nobody's looking at you, and I'm sure that's true, but knowing it hasn't ever changed what my body does.

The clearest test of this was my cousin's wedding last year. There were about a hundred and twenty people, the floor filled up around ten, and I stayed at the table for the entire evening. What surprised me is that I had a genuinely good night. I talked to an aunt I hadn't seen in six years, I ate two desserts, and I watched my uncle — a man who cannot dance at all — enjoy himself completely for about forty minutes. Two people tried to pull me up and I said no both times without feeling bad about it, which I couldn't have done ten years ago.

So I'd put it this way: I like dancing enormously as a thing that happens in a room I'm in. I've just accepted that my part in it is watching, and honestly, at a wedding somebody has to be the person holding the drinks.
说实话，不喜欢——至少不喜欢在人前跳。厨房里没人的时候我跳得挺开心，但只要有观众，我身上就有个开关被关掉了。我已经接受了这一点，而不是想着去改。
原因其实很简单：我没办法不盯着自己看。大部分我喜欢的事情，我做的时候会陷进去，忘了有人在看；跳舞正好相反，我全程都在给自己的胳膊做解说，而那个解说从来不客气。我知道大家常说的是“根本没人看你”，我相信这话是对的，但知道归知道，我的身体从来没因此改变过。
最能说明这一点的是去年我表姐的婚礼。大概一百二十个人，十点左右舞池就满了，而我整晚都坐在桌边。让我意外的是，那一晚我过得是真的开心。我和一个六年没见的阿姨聊了很久，吃了两份甜点，还看着我舅舅——一个完全不会跳舞的人——尽兴地跳了差不多四十分钟。有两个人来拉我上去，我两次都说了不，而且一点也不觉得抱歉，这在十年前我做不到。
所以我会这么说：作为一件在我所在的房间里发生的事，我非常喜欢跳舞，只是我接受了自己的角色是看。而且说实话，婚礼上总得有个人负责看着大家的酒杯。
Constantly, with people I know well — and never with people I don't, which I think is a fairly universal line even though nobody explains it to you.

The reason I like it is that sharing plates is about half of why I enjoy eating out at all. If everybody orders one thing and eats only that, you've each had one dish, and you've had a meal in parallel rather than together. Passing things around means the table has eaten eight things, and it also means the conversation keeps getting interrupted in a good way — somebody's reaction to something is a much better prompt than the question you were about to ask.

My friends and I have had an unspoken rule about this for years: everything on the table belongs to everybody. It started, I think, because one of us always ordered badly and we got tired of watching him regret it. Now it's automatic — nobody asks, plates get turned so the good side faces out, and if somebody orders something nobody else wanted, that person has made a decision on behalf of the group. The one time it broke down was with a colleague who didn't know the rule and watched, visibly alarmed, as her food was distributed.

So my answer depends entirely on the company rather than on the food. With the right people I'd taste anything. With people I've just met I wouldn't reach across the table for money, because the whole thing only works when nobody has to be brave about it.
和很熟的人一起吃饭时会一直尝，和不熟的人则完全不会。我觉得这条界线其实相当普遍，虽然从来没人跟你解释过。
我喜欢这样的原因是，分着吃差不多是我喜欢在外面吃饭的一半理由。如果每个人点一道、只吃自己那道，那你们各自吃了一道菜，是并排吃饭，而不是一起吃饭。互相传着吃意味着这一桌吃到了八样东西，而且它还会不断打断谈话——是那种好的打断：别人对某样东西的反应，比你原本准备问的问题好用得多。
我和朋友之间有一条心照不宣的规矩，很多年了：桌上所有东西都是大家的。我记得起因是我们中间有一个人总是点得很糟，我们看他后悔看烦了。现在这已经是自动的了——没人会问，盘子会被转过来把好的一面朝外；如果有人点了一样别人都不想要的，那这个人就是替全组做了个决定。唯一一次失灵，是一个不知道这条规矩的同事，眼看着自己的菜被分掉，脸上明显有点慌。
所以我的答案完全取决于和谁一起吃，而不是吃什么。和对的人在一起，我什么都愿意尝；和刚认识的人在一起，给我钱我也不会伸手去夹。因为这整件事只有在没人需要鼓起勇气的时候才成立。

Two, and they're deliberately at opposite ends: a long breakfast on Saturday morning, and a proper clean on Sunday evening. Everything between them is unplanned, which only works because those two are fixed.

The reason I hold onto them is that without something anchoring each end, I spend the whole weekend deciding what to do with the weekend, and that turns out to be more tiring than working. Having a known start means Saturday doesn't drift until eleven. Having a known finish means Sunday night isn't the low, anxious hour it used to be — the dread I used to feel then was mostly about walking into a mess on Monday, and it turns out that's a solvable problem rather than a mood.

The breakfast is the one I'd defend hardest. It takes about an hour, I cook something that needs a pan rather than a toaster, and I don't look at my phone for any of it. That last part is the whole thing — I tried the same ritual with the phone on the table and it collapsed within a month, because an hour with a phone in it is just four fifteen-minute stretches. The clean is less romantic: two hours, music on, and I do the kitchen properly rather than adequately. I've been doing both for about three years now and I've missed maybe six weekends total.
So I'd say routines like these aren't a restriction on a weekend, they're what stops one disappearing. The unstructured middle is only enjoyable because it's bounded by something.
两个，而且我故意把它们放在两头：周六早上一顿很长的早饭，周日晚上认真打扫一次。中间的时间完全没有计划，而这之所以行得通，正是因为两头是固定的。
我坚持这两件事的原因是，如果两头都没有东西固定住，我会把整个周末花在“决定周末做什么”上面，而那比上班还累。有一个确定的开始，周六就不会一直拖到十一点；有一个确定的结尾，周日晚上就不再是以前那种低落又焦虑的时段——我以前那种不安，其实大部分是因为怕周一走进一片乱，而这原来是个能解决的问题，不是一种情绪。
早饭是我会拼命守住的那一个。大概要一个小时，我会做需要用锅的东西，而不是烤面包机，而且全程不看手机。最后这一点才是关键——我试过把手机放在桌上做同样的事，一个月之内就垮了，因为一个有手机的小时其实只是四个十五分钟。打扫就没那么浪漫了：两个小时，放着音乐，厨房要认真做，而不是差不多就行。这两件事我坚持了大概三年，一共可能只断过六个周末。
所以我会说，这样的习惯不是对周末的限制，而是让周末不至于消失的东西。中间那段没有安排的时间之所以享受，正是因为它被两头框住了。

The ones I actually return to are all novels about fairly ordinary people doing fairly ordinary things. I went through a period of reading much more ambitious books and I can remember admiring them, but I can't remember any of them.

The reason, I think, is that a big plot gives me nothing to hold onto afterwards. I follow it, I get to the end, and a month later it's gone. Whereas a character who reminds me of somebody I actually know stays, because every time I see that person I get the book back. It's a slightly parasitic way to read — I'm using the novel to think about my own life — but I've stopped pretending otherwise.

The clearest case is a family novel I've now read three times, roughly five years apart. The first time I read it I was about twenty and I thought it was about the daughter, because I was the daughter's age. At thirty I read it again and it was obviously about the mother, and I was slightly shocked that I'd missed her entirely. The third time, last year, the person I couldn't stop watching was the uncle, who I'd previously registered as more or less furniture. Same book, three different books. I don't think that happens with plot.

So what I look for in fiction is recognition rather than surprise. A book that surprises me is enjoyable once. A book that recognises somebody I know is something I can go back to as I become different people, and that's a much better return on three hundred pages.
我真正会重读的，基本都是写普通人做普通事的小说。我也有过一段时间读那些野心大得多的书，我记得自己很佩服它们，但内容一点都想不起来了。
我觉得原因是，宏大的情节读完之后不给我留下任何可以抓住的东西。我跟着读，读到结尾，一个月后就没了。而一个让我想起身边某个真实的人的角色会留下来，因为每次我见到那个人，那本书就回来了。这种读法其实有点“寄生”——我是在借小说想我自己的生活——但我已经不装作不是这样了。
最清楚的例子是一本写家庭的小说，我到现在读了三遍，大概每隔五年一次。第一次读的时候我二十岁左右，我以为那本书写的是女儿，因为我和女儿差不多大。三十岁再读，它明显写的是母亲，我还挺震惊自己第一次完全没看见她。第三次是去年，我一直盯着看的人变成了那个舅舅，而他在我之前的印象里差不多等于家具。同一本书，三本不同的书。我觉得情节做不到这一点。
所以我在小说里找的是熟悉感，而不是意外。一本让我意外的书，好看一次；一本认出了我身边某个人的书，是我可以在自己变成不同的人之后再回去的东西，而这三百页的回报要高得多。
A cat we had for fourteen years, called Mimi. There were other animals in the house at various points, but she's the only one I'd describe as mine rather than the family's.

The reason she mattered so much is that she was the first thing that ever properly depended on me. I was eight, and my parents made a point of handing over the feeding rather than doing it themselves, which at the time felt like a chore and in hindsight was obviously deliberate. Being the person an animal comes to when it's hungry changes something in a child — you stop being the one who is looked after and become, in one small area, the one doing the looking after.

She arrived when I was eight and died when I was twenty-two, which means she was there for essentially all of the parts of my life I can remember properly. She was in the room when I did my exams. She was there when I came home from university at Christmas and she'd got noticeably slower each time. At the end she was deaf and would sleep on the warm bit of the floor by the radiator, and my father — who had spent fourteen years announcing that he was not a cat person — was the one who sat with her.

So I don't really think of her as a pet in memory. She's more like a measuring stick: she was the constant across everything that changed between eight and twenty-two, and I notice I date things by her without meaning to.
一只我们养了十四年的猫，叫咪咪。家里前后也有过别的动物，但只有她我会说是“我的”，而不是“我们家的”。
她之所以那么重要，是因为她是第一个真正依赖我的生命。我当时八岁，我父母特意把喂食这件事交给我，而不是自己做。那时候我只觉得是个麻烦事，现在回头看当然是故意的。当一只动物饿了会来找你，这会改变一个孩子身上的某些东西——你不再只是被照顾的那一个，而是在某个很小的范围里，变成了照顾别人的那一个。
她来我们家的时候我八岁，走的时候我二十二岁，也就是说，我能清楚记得的人生阶段，她几乎全程都在。我考试的时候她在房间里；我大学放寒假回家，每一次都能明显看出她又慢了一些。到最后她耳朵聋了，喜欢睡在暖气旁边地板发热的那一块，而我父亲——那个用了十四年宣布自己不喜欢猫的人——是最后陪着她的那个。
所以在记忆里我不太把她当成宠物，她更像一把尺子：从八岁到二十二岁，别的都在变，只有她是不变的那一个。我发现自己会不自觉地拿她来给事情标记时间。
A noodle place about four minutes from my office, which I go to far more often than I would admit unprompted. I've ordered the same thing there for two years.

The reason it wins isn't that it's the best food nearby — it clearly isn't. It's the only place within walking distance that can feed me in under ten minutes without producing regret an hour later. That's a narrower category than you'd think. Fast tends to mean heavy, and light tends to mean a twenty-five-minute wait, and at one o'clock on a Tuesday I have neither the time nor the willingness to make a decision about it.

I go about twice a week and I order the same bowl every time. The man behind the counter started nodding at me instead of taking the order somewhere around month four, which I found unreasonably pleasant. I did try a different thing on the menu once, about a year in, and it was fine, and I have never done it again. I think part of what I'm buying there is the absence of a choice — by one o'clock I've made enough decisions and I want the next twenty minutes to contain none.
So it's a favourite on speed and consistency rather than on quality, and I've made my peace with that. There's better food within fifteen minutes' walk. There is nothing better within four.
我公司走路四分钟的一家面馆，我去的频率比我主动承认的高得多。同一样东西我在那儿点了两年。
它之所以胜出，不是因为附近数它最好吃——显然不是。而是因为它是走得到的地方里唯一一家能在十分钟内让我吃饱、而且一小时后不会后悔的店。这个类别比你以为的窄：快通常意味着油，清淡通常意味着等二十五分钟。而在周二下午一点，我既没有时间，也没有意愿去为这件事做决定。
我大概一周去两次，每次点同一碗。柜台后面那位大哥大概在第四个月开始，看见我就点头，而不再问我要什么了——这让我觉得高兴得有点没道理。大概一年的时候我确实试过菜单上的另一样，还行，然后我再没试过第二次。我想我在那儿买的东西里，有一部分正是“没有选择”——到一点的时候我已经做了足够多的决定，我希望接下来的二十分钟里一个都不用做。
所以它赢在快和稳定，而不是好吃，我也接受了这一点。走十五分钟范围内有更好吃的，但走四分钟范围内没有更好的。
I doodle constantly and I cannot draw at all, and I've come to think those two things are much less related than the question assumes.

The distinction is that one is a skill I never acquired and the other is a way of thinking with a pen in my hand. Drawing is an attempt to produce a likeness of something. Doodling isn't representing anything — it's what my hand does while the rest of me is listening, and the evidence that it's doing something useful is that I follow meetings noticeably better when I'm doing it. I spent years assuming this looked rude and then read that it's fairly well established as an attention aid, which was a relief.

Every notebook I've used in a meeting has margins full of boxes and arrows, and none of them mean anything at all. They're not diagrams of what's being discussed — I've checked. It's the same six shapes in different arrangements, and the density goes up when the meeting is boring, which makes it a fairly reliable record of how a two-hour session actually went. A colleague once asked to see my notes and I had to explain that the useful part was four lines and the rest was structural.

So I'd say I like the habit rather than the drawing. If somebody handed me a pencil and asked for a picture of a house I'd produce something a six-year-old would be disappointed by, and I've made no attempt in twenty years to change that.
我经常随手涂鸦，同时完全不会画画。我逐渐觉得，这两件事的关联比这个问题所假设的要小得多。
区别在于：一个是我从来没学过的技能，另一个是我手里拿着笔时的一种思考方式。画画是试图画出某样东西的样子；涂鸦不表现任何东西——那只是我在听别人说话时，我的手在做的事。而它确实有用的证据是：我一边涂一边开会，明显跟得更清楚。我有好多年以为这看起来很不礼貌，后来读到这在心理学上其实是被认可的一种注意力辅助方式，松了一口气。
我开会用过的每一个本子，页边上都画满了方块和箭头，而它们没有任何含义。它们不是在会上讨论内容的示意图——我专门检查过。就是同样的六种形状换着排列，而且会越无聊画得越密，所以它反倒成了一份挺可靠的记录，能看出一场两小时的会实际上是怎么过的。有一次同事想看我的笔记，我得跟他解释：有用的部分是四行，剩下的都是结构性的。
所以我会说，我喜欢的是这个习惯，而不是画画本身。如果有人递给我一支铅笔让我画一栋房子，我画出来的东西会让一个六岁小孩失望，而这二十年里我没做过任何改变它的努力。

Almost all of them are comedies I watched with my family rather than anything I picked on my own. Which is slightly awkward to admit, because it means my taste at that age was really just whatever four people could agree on.

The reason those are the ones that stuck is that the programme was never the point. It was the only reliable hour in the week when everybody in the house was in the same room and nobody was arguing. My parents worked shifts that didn't line up, so we didn't eat together most days. Friday at eight was the exception, and I think we all quietly protected it without ever saying so.

There was one series in particular that we watched every Friday for about three years. I could tell you the theme tune now, twenty years later, and I still quote one specific line to my brother whenever he's being unreasonable — he says it back, and neither of us has to explain anything. When it finished, we tried two or three replacements and none of them took, and that was more or less the end of the ritual. I was fifteen by then and starting to be out on Fridays anyway, so it probably would have ended regardless.

So if you ask me what my favourite show was, the honest answer is that I'm not really describing a programme. I'm describing a sofa, and four people on it, and the specific relief of a house where nobody was in a bad mood for half an hour.
几乎全是和家人一起看的喜剧，而不是我自己挑的，承认这一点还有点不好意思，因为这意味着我那个年纪的品味，其实就是四个人能达成一致的东西。
那些之所以留了下来，是因为节目本身从来不是重点。那是一周里唯一可靠的一个小时，全家人在同一个房间里，而且没人在吵架。我父母上的班倒不到一起，所以大多数日子我们不一起吃饭。周五晚上八点是例外，我想我们几个都在悄悄守着它，只是谁都没说出口。
有一部剧我们连着看了差不多三年，每周五一集。二十年过去了，那个主题曲我现在还能哼出来，而且每次我弟弟不讲道理的时候，我还会引用里面某一句台词——他会用同一句回我，我们谁都不用解释什么。那部剧完结之后，我们试过两三部替代的，都没接上，那基本也就是这个习惯的终点了。那时候我十五岁，周五本来也开始往外跑了，所以大概怎么样都会结束。
所以你问我最喜欢的电视节目是什么，老实的回答是：我说的其实不是一个节目，而是一张沙发、沙发上的四个人，以及那种“有半个小时家里没人心情不好”的踏实感。
In bed, late, with one lamp on and the rest of the room dark. I've tried to become the sort of person who reads in a chair by a window in the afternoon and it has never once worked.

The reason is availability rather than comfort. Late at night is the only hour in my day when nobody could reasonably want anything from me — no message needs answering at half past eleven, and if it does, that's genuinely somebody else's emergency. Every other reading spot I've tried competes with something. A chair in the afternoon competes with the idea that I could be doing something useful, and that idea always wins.

In practice it's about thirty or forty pages a night, which sounds small but works out at a book every couple of weeks, or roughly twenty-five books a year. I read paper for this specifically, because the one experiment I ran with reading on a tablet in bed lasted about three weeks before I was just on the internet in the dark. I also keep the next book on the table rather than in a pile, because I've learned that if choosing what to read next is a decision I have to make at eleven at night, I'll choose sleep.

So the honest answer is that the place matters much less than the hour. If I could get the same guaranteed uninterrupted stretch at eight in the morning, I'd read at eight in the morning — it's just that nobody has ever offered me one.
在床上，晚一点，只开一盏灯，房间里其他地方都是暗的。我努力想变成那种下午坐在窗边椅子上看书的人，但一次都没成功过。
原因不是舒服，而是“有没有空”。深夜是我一天里唯一一段没有人有理由来找我的时间——十一点半没有什么消息非回不可，如果真有，那也确实是别人的急事。我试过的每一个别的看书地点，都要和别的东西竞争：下午坐在椅子上，要和“我本可以做点有用的事”这个念头竞争，而那个念头每次都赢。
实际上我一晚大概读三四十页，听起来不多，但差不多两个星期一本书，一年大概二十五本。我专门用纸质书看这个时段，因为我唯一一次试过在床上用平板看书，坚持了大概三个星期，之后就变成在黑暗里上网了。我还会把下一本书放在床头桌上，而不是堆在书堆里，因为我发现如果“下一本读什么”是我十一点还得做的决定，那我一定会选择睡觉。
所以老实的回答是：地点远没有时段重要。如果早上八点也能有同样一段保证不被打断的时间，我就会在早上八点读书——只是从来没人给过我这样一段时间。

I do, but deliberately much less than I used to, and I'd argue I'm better informed for it. For about three years I had news on constantly — first thing in the morning, in queues, last thing at night — and I've cut that down to roughly twenty minutes a day.

The reason is that the constant version was producing anxiety without producing understanding. If you check every hour, what you get is the same story in eight slightly different states of incompleteness, and your brain treats each version as new information when it isn't. I also noticed I could tell you what had happened but not why it mattered, which is a strange kind of ignorance to arrive at through effort.

What I do now is read one long piece in the morning — something that took someone a week to write rather than twenty minutes — and then nothing until the next day. No notifications, no app on the home screen. The first fortnight was genuinely uncomfortable; I kept reaching for the phone out of habit and feeling like I was missing something. By the second month that had gone entirely. The test for me was a conversation about six weeks in where I realised I could actually explain the background of a story rather than just the headline, and I hadn't been able to do that for years.

So my view is that the question isn't whether to follow the news, it's what unit you follow it in. Hourly is a diet of fragments. Daily and long-form is a diet of arguments, and only one of those leaves you able to say anything.
会关注，但比以前刻意少了很多，而且我认为这样反而更了解情况。有大概三年时间我是一直开着新闻的——早上第一件事、排队的时候、睡前最后一件事；现在我把它压缩到一天大约二十分钟。
原因是，那种一直看的方式只制造焦虑，不产生理解。如果你每小时刷一次，你得到的是同一件事的八个稍微不同的、都不完整的版本，而你的大脑会把每一个版本都当成新信息，其实并不是。我还注意到，我能告诉你发生了什么，却说不出它为什么重要——靠努力得到这样一种无知，是挺奇怪的。
我现在的做法是，早上读一篇长文章——那种别人花了一周写出来的，而不是二十分钟写出来的——然后到第二天为止都不看了。关掉通知，主屏幕上不放新闻应用。头两个星期是真的难受，我总是习惯性地去摸手机，觉得自己错过了什么；到第二个月就完全没有这种感觉了。对我来说的检验是大概六周后的一次聊天，我发现自己能讲清楚一件事的来龙去脉，而不只是标题，这种能力我已经好几年没有了。
所以我的看法是：问题不是要不要关注新闻，而是你用多大的单位去关注。按小时是一堆碎片，按天、读长文章是一套论证，而只有后者能让你说出点什么来。

I love it now, but that's an acquired position rather than a natural one. As a child I couldn't handle anything at all, and my family still brings up a meal where I drank three glasses of water and gave up on a dish that, by any reasonable standard, was not spicy.

What changed my mind was understanding that heat isn't really a flavour on its own — it's what carries everything else. A simple dish with the right amount of chilli in it tastes like somebody made a decision. The same dish without it can taste like a collection of ingredients that happened to end up in the same bowl. There's also a physical thing: it slows you down. You can't eat something properly hot quickly, so you end up sitting at the table longer and talking more.

The turning point was the first time I ate real Sichuan food, at about twenty-four. Somebody ordered for the table and I genuinely could not finish my portion — I got maybe two-thirds through and had to stop, sweating, while everyone else carried on talking. What struck me was that they weren't enduring it, they were enjoying it, and I could tell the difference. I went back to the same place four or five times over the next year deliberately building up. Now there's a jar of chilli oil that lives on my table permanently and goes on things it has no business going on.
So it's less a preference than a skill I decided to acquire, and I'd say to anyone who thinks they can't take spice that they're probably about eight meals away from being able to.
现在很喜欢，但这是练出来的，不是天生的。我小时候一点辣都吃不了，我家里人到现在还会提起有一顿饭，我喝了三杯水，最后放弃了一道按任何标准都算不上辣的菜。
让我改变想法的，是我后来明白了辣本身其实不算一种味道，它是承载别的味道的东西。一道简单的菜，辣度合适，吃起来就像有人做过决定；同一道菜没有辣，可能就像一堆碰巧进了同一个碗的食材。还有一点是身体上的：辣会让你慢下来。真正够辣的东西你吃不快，于是你在桌边坐得更久，话也说得更多。
转折点是我大概二十四岁那年第一次吃正宗川菜。有人替全桌点了菜，我是真的吃不完自己那份——大概吃了三分之二就得停下来，一头汗，而其他人还在照常聊天。让我震动的是，他们不是在忍，是在享受，这两者我分得出来。之后一年里我特意又去了那家店四五次，一点点往上加。现在我家餐桌上常年放着一罐辣椒油，还会被我放到一些根本不该放的东西上。
所以与其说这是口味偏好，不如说是我决定去学的一项技能。我想对所有觉得自己吃不了辣的人说：你大概只差八顿饭。
I used to, fairly heavily, and I've almost entirely stopped. Not as a principle I adopted — it happened as a result of one small change that I made for a completely different reason.

The reason I stopped is that being permanently reachable was making me slower during the week, not faster. If a message can arrive at any moment, you never fully put anything down, and a Tuesday afternoon where you're half-expecting an interruption is worth less than one where you aren't. I'd assumed the availability was a favour I was doing everyone. It's closer to the truth that I was spreading a fixed amount of attention over seven days instead of five and getting less out of it.

The change was taking email off my phone in January. I did it because the phone was full and I was deleting things, which is an embarrassingly unheroic origin for what turned out to be the most useful work decision I've made. I expected consequences. There have been none. Nobody has mentioned it. Two people have my number for genuine emergencies and neither has used it. The holiday test was in August — nine days, and I came back to about sixty emails, of which four still needed anything and none of them had been urgent by the time I read them.

So the thing I'd say to anyone considering it is that the availability almost certainly matters far less than you think. I was carrying it around for years on the assumption that removing it would cost something, and the actual cost, as far as I can measure, was zero.
以前会，而且相当频繁，现在几乎完全不了。这不是我主动确立的什么原则，而是我出于完全不同的理由做了一个小改动之后的结果。
我不再这样做的原因是：随时能被找到，让我平时的效率变低了，而不是变高。如果消息随时可能进来，你就永远没法把任何东西彻底放下，而一个你半悬着等打断的周二下午，价值低于一个不用等的周二下午。我原本以为“随时在线”是我在帮所有人的忙，更接近事实的说法是：我把一份固定的注意力摊到了七天而不是五天上，结果得到的更少了。
那个改动是我一月份把邮箱从手机上删掉了。我这么做是因为手机存储满了，我在删东西——作为“我做过的最有用的工作决定”的起因，这实在有点上不了台面。我本来预计会有后果，结果一个都没有。没有人提起过这件事。有两个人有我的电话号码，可以在真正的急事时找我，两个人都没用过。真正的检验是八月份的假期：九天，回来时大概有六十封邮件，其中还需要处理的有四封，而且到我读的时候没有一封还是紧急的。
所以我想对任何正在考虑这件事的人说：那份“随时可用”几乎肯定远没有你以为的重要。我背着它背了好几年，一直假设拿掉它会有代价；而就我能衡量的范围而言，实际的代价是零。
One person — a musician — and the town has spent about twenty-five years making sure nobody forgets it. I could tell you his name before I could tell you the name of the local MP.

The reason it looms so large is that in a small place a single success stops being one person's and becomes a kind of shared property. Nobody in a city claims a famous person the way a town of eleven thousand does. There's a logic to it too: if somebody who went to your school and worked in your shops can do that, then the place isn't a dead end, and everybody in it gets to feel slightly differently about where they live. That's a lot of work for one person's career to be doing.

The illustration I always give is the café where he apparently worked for one summer when he was seventeen. There's a photograph of him on the wall, and it's been there for at least twenty years — the frame is sun-bleached on one side. He has, as far as anyone knows, been back to the town twice. The café has changed hands at least once and the photograph stayed, which tells you it's not sentimental, it's part of the fittings.

So he's less a celebrity there than a landmark. People give directions using that café. I doubt he knows, and I suspect if he did he'd find it either touching or slightly claustrophobic, and I'm not sure which I'd feel.
有一个，是个音乐人，而我们那儿花了大概二十五年确保没有人会忘记这件事。我能说出他的名字，比我能说出当地人大代表的名字要快。
它之所以份量这么重，是因为在小地方，一个人的成功会不再属于他自己，而变成一种共同财产。一个城市里的人不会像一个一万一千人的小城那样去“认领”一个名人。这里面也有它的道理：如果一个上过你们那所学校、在你们那些店里打过工的人能做到，那这个地方就不是死胡同，住在这儿的每个人对自己所在的地方就能有点不一样的感觉。这对一个人的事业来说，是相当重的负担。
我常举的例子是那家咖啡馆——据说他十七岁那年在那儿打过一个夏天的工。墙上挂着他的照片，至少挂了二十年，相框有一侧已经被太阳晒褪色了。就大家所知，他后来只回过这个小城两次。那家咖啡馆至少换过一次老板，而照片留了下来，这就说明它不是什么感情用事，它已经属于店里的固定装修了。
所以在那里他与其说是名人，不如说是一个地标——大家指路时会说“那家咖啡馆”。我怀疑他并不知道，而且我猜如果他知道了，会觉得要么很温暖，要么有点透不过气，我也说不准我自己会是哪一种。
Somewhere cold and nearly empty — a northern coastline in winter, with almost nobody in the shot. Which is not what the genre usually does, and that's most of the appeal.

The reason is that action films have started to look interchangeable, and I think it's because they're nearly all shot in warm cities. You get glass, traffic, crowds and heat, and after twenty minutes it doesn't matter which city it is. A cold empty place does a lot of the work for you: it establishes that help is far away and that the environment itself is a problem, and it does both without a single line of dialogue explaining the stakes.

The specific place I have in mind is a stretch of coast I visited a few years ago in late autumn. The weather changed four times in one day — clear, then a wall of fog, then rain coming sideways, then completely still. I was there about six hours and I came away thinking that if you filmed a chase along that road you'd barely need to design anything. There was also almost no sound except wind, which I noticed because it's so rare, and silence is a much better tool for tension than a score is.

So I'd choose the location for what it does to the mood rather than for what it lets you stage. Most of the memorable sequences I can think of are memorable because of where they happen, and the stunts are the part I've forgotten.
一个又冷又几乎没有人的地方——冬天的北方海岸线，画面里几乎不出现人。这不是这个类型片通常的做法，而这正是它吸引我的大部分原因。
原因是动作片现在看起来越来越像是可以互换的，我觉得这是因为它们几乎都在温暖的城市里拍。你看到的是玻璃、车流、人群和热气，二十分钟以后你根本分不出那是哪座城市。而一个寒冷空旷的地方能替你完成很多工作：它一下子确立了“救援离得很远”和“环境本身就是个问题”这两件事，而且不需要一句解释处境的台词。
我心里想的那个具体地点，是几年前深秋我去过的一段海岸。那里的天气一天变了四次——先是晴，然后是一堵雾墙，接着是横着下的雨，最后完全静下来。我在那儿待了大概六个小时，离开时的想法是：如果在那条路上拍一场追逐，你几乎不需要额外设计什么。而且那里除了风声几乎没有别的声音，我之所以注意到，是因为这太罕见了——而营造紧张感，安静比配乐好用得多。
所以我选景是看它能带来什么气氛，而不是看它方便调度什么动作。我能想起来的那些让人难忘的段落，几乎都是因为发生的地点而难忘，而动作本身恰恰是我忘掉的那部分。
I do, and it's the only personal object on my desk, which makes it slightly conspicuous in a way I didn't plan.

The reason it's there has turned out to be more about other people than about me. In a large open office you need something that makes a conversation easy to start, because the alternative is that people walk past for two years without ever having a reason to stop. A photograph does that work. It's a low-stakes thing to ask about, it doesn't require the other person to know anything, and it gives them a way out if they'd rather not talk — they can just glance at it and keep walking.

The evidence is fairly blunt: more colleagues have asked me about my dog than have ever asked me about anything I've actually produced. I know the names of two people's cats and one person's rabbit as a direct result of conversations that started at my desk. Sheepdog trials, which most people have never watched and which I'd argue is one of the strangest and best things you can see in a field.

The reason it fascinates me is that it's the only sport I know of where the entire event depends on two species understanding each other at distance. The handler can't touch the dog, can't be near it, and communicates through whistles across a couple of hundred metres. The sheep, meanwhile, have not agreed to any of this. So you're watching a plan being executed by an animal that grasps the objective, on animals that don't, by a person who can only suggest.

I saw one at a country fair when I was about nine and I still remember being surprised by how little the handler moved. I'd expected shouting and running. He stood almost completely still for six or seven minutes. The drama was entirely in the dog — the way it would drop flat and wait, then move a few metres and stop again, adjusting for something in the sheep's behaviour that I certainly couldn't see. At the end the applause was noticeably restrained, and I've since worked out that's because clapping loudly is unhelpful to everyone involved.

So what appeals to me is the communication rather than the competition. It's the only sport I can think of where the impressive thing isn't strength or speed, it's two very different minds getting a shared job done with almost no shared language.
牧羊犬比赛。大多数人都没看过，而我认为这是你在一片草地上能看到的最奇怪、也最好的事情之一。

One local club, and no national team at all — which surprises people, because the national side is the one you're supposed to care about.

一支本地的球队，国家队完全不关注——这一点常常让人意外，因为按理说国家队才是你该在意的那个。

It's busier, noisier and, on balance, considerably better — which isn't what I expected to end up saying, because for about ten years I told everyone it had been ruined.

That produced a town where everyone was either under twenty or over sixty, and the middle was hollow. Whatever combination of remote work and cheap rent reversed that, it has changed the character of the place far more than any development has.

更热闹、更吵，总的来说也好了不少——这不是我原本以为自己会说的话，因为有大概十年时间，我逢人就说我们那儿被毁了。

Who lives there. The buildings are almost all the same ones, which is the thing that makes the change so disorienting when you visit.

The reason it feels strange is that a place that has been physically rebuilt gives you permission to feel it's different. This one hasn't. The shape of the street is identical, the corners are where they were, the postbox hasn't moved — and every single household behind those identical doors is somebody else. The families I grew up around have gone almost without exception, mostly for the ordinary reason that people who bought in their thirties are now in their seventies and have moved to be near their children.

I walked down my old street last year — I hadn't done it properly in about eight years — and I counted. Thirty houses. I recognised one door, and only because the family who live there now bought it from people I knew and kept the same colour. The children on the pavement were the age I was when I lived there, which is an obvious thing to happen and still lands oddly. Two front gardens that had been gardens are now parking.

So the place looks entirely familiar and feels like somewhere I've never been, and I think that combination is more unsettling than straightforward redevelopment would be. If they'd knocked it down I'd have grieved once and been done with it.
住的人变了。房子几乎还是原来那些，而这恰恰是回去的时候最让人恍惚的地方。

A vet, and I held onto it with total conviction until I was about twelve, which is longer than most children keep the first answer.

That's a fairly sophisticated piece of reasoning for an eight-year-old and I don't remember making it, but it's clearly what was going on. I wasn't drawn to medicine at all. I was drawn to a life where the thing I liked wasn't confined to evenings and weekends.

I had a notebook. 兽医，而且我抱着这个想法一直抱到十二岁左右，比大多数孩子守住第一个答案的时间都长。

Yes, and I'd keep them at the weekend as well — though I accept that both of those positions cost somebody money, which is why neither is universal.

The reason I'd keep finals outdoors is that weather is part of the sport rather than an interference with it. Move a final indoors and you get a cleaner contest and a less interesting one, because you've removed a variable that both sides have to solve in real time. The strongest argument against me is the spectator's — people have paid a great deal and travelled a long way, and telling them to get wet for the sake of the narrative is easy when it isn't your evening.

The best final I've ever watched was played in genuinely heavy rain, and it is the only one from that decade I can still describe. The conditions turned it into a completely different game — the technically better side couldn't play their normal way and visibly didn't know what to do about it, and something that would have been a routine result became watchable for two hours. People still bring it up. I've watched three or four cleaner, higher-quality finals since and I couldn't tell you the score of any of them.

So I'd accept the risk of a ruined match for the chance of a memorable one, and I'd argue the sport is better off over a decade for doing that. A guaranteed decent event forgotten in a fortnight is worth less than an occasional disaster that people are still arguing about ten years later.
我觉得应该，而且我也会安排在周末——不过我承认这两个立场都会让某些人少赚钱，所以它们都不是共识。

我看过最精彩的一场决赛就是在瓢泼大雨里踢的，也是那十年里唯一一场我到现在还能描述出来的。那种条件把它变成了一场完全不同的比赛——技术更好的那一方没法按他们平时的方式踢，而且明显不知道该怎么办；一场本来会是常规结果的比赛，变成了两个小时都挪不开眼的东西。到现在还有人提起它。那之后我看过三四场更干净、质量更高的决赛，但没有一场我说得出比分。
所以我愿意冒着比赛被毁掉的风险，去换一场值得记住的比赛。而且我认为，把十年放在一起看，这项运动因此是更好的：一个保证过得去、两个星期就被忘掉的赛事，价值低于一场偶然的灾难——那种十年之后大家还在争论的灾难。
The light in the front room between about three and five in the afternoon. Which is a slightly strange thing to name, because it's the one feature I had absolutely nothing to do with.

It matters to me because it was invisible in the process of choosing the place. When you look at flats you're shown photographs taken at whatever hour suited the agent, and you're comparing floor area and how far it is to the station — measurable things. Nobody can photograph what a room feels like at four o'clock in October, and it turns out that's the thing I'd now weight highest if I ever moved again.

The proof is that I've rearranged the room twice to sit in it. My desk was originally against the far wall, which was the sensible place for it — plug sockets, no glare on the screen. 下午三点到五点之间，客厅里的那片光。说出来有点奇怪，因为这恰恰是我完全没有参与决定的一个特点。

证据是我为了坐在那片光里，把房间重新布置了两次。我的桌子本来靠在最里面那面墙，那是最合理的位置——有插座，屏幕也不反光。住了大概半年后我把它挪到窗边，后来又往左挪了三十厘米，因为第一个位置到四点半就照不到了。我的伴侣觉得这是一种很荒唐的决定家具位置的方式。但我一周有三天在家工作，而那一个半小时是我一天里真正期待的部分。
所以我最喜欢我家的地方，是我当初没法刻意挑到的那一点。我把这当成一个提醒，提醒我平时是怎么做选择的：我看房时列的清单上有十一项，而最后真正重要的那一项，一项都没在上面。
Cleaning up other people's spreadsheets. I'm aware of how that sounds. I've had colleagues look at me with genuine concern when they realised I wasn't joking.

The reason I like it is that it has a clear before and an after, and startlingly little work does. Most of what I do is contributing to something that will be judged in six months by criteria that haven't been agreed yet. A messy file, by contrast, is unambiguously broken at nine o'clock and unambiguously fixed by three, and everybody can see it. I think what I'm actually enjoying is the certainty rather than the spreadsheet, and I've stopped being embarrassed about needing some of that in a week.

The clearest instance was a weekend about two years ago. A colleague had a data file with four years of records in it that had been maintained by six different people, none of whom had agreed on a date format. It wasn't my project and nobody asked me. I did it on a Saturday, for free, entirely because knowing it was in that state was bothering me in the way a picture hanging crooked bothers some people. It took about five hours and I enjoyed all five. She thought I'd lost my mind and then used it every week for the next two years.
So it isn't the subject matter — I have no particular interest in data. It's that finished actually means finished, and there is very little else in an adult working life about which that's true.
整理别人做的表格。我知道这话听起来是什么感觉。有同事在意识到我不是在开玩笑之后，看我的眼神里是真的带着担心。
我喜欢它的原因是它有清清楚楚的“之前”和“之后”，而有这个属性的工作少得惊人。我做的大部分事情，都是在为某个六个月后才会被评价的东西添砖加瓦，而评价标准到现在都还没定。相比之下，一个乱掉的文件在九点是毫无疑问地坏着的，到三点是毫无疑问地好了的，而且所有人都看得见。我想我真正享受的是那份确定性，而不是表格本身。我也不再为自己一周需要一点这种东西而不好意思了。
最清楚的一次是大概两年前的一个周末。一位同事有一个存了四年记录的数据文件，前后由六个人维护过，而这六个人没有一个在日期格式上达成过一致。那不是我的项目，也没有人来找我。我在一个周六做完了它，没有报酬，纯粹是因为知道它是那个状态让我难受，就像有些人受不了一幅挂歪的画。那花了大概五个小时，五个小时我都很享受。她当时觉得我疯了，然后接下来两年里每周都在用它。
所以这跟内容无关——我对数据本身没有任何特别的兴趣。而是“做完了”真的意味着做完了，而在一个成年人的职业生活里，符合这一条的东西实在太少了。
A strategy game I've been playing on and off for about fifteen years. Not continuously — I'll go eight months without opening it and then play for three weeks.

The reason it has outlasted everything else is that it's slow enough to stop in the middle of. Almost nothing else respects that. Most games are built to make putting them down feel like a loss — a run you'll have to restart, a timer that keeps running while you're away. This one just waits. I can close it mid-turn and come back in March and lose nothing, and it turns out that's the single feature that determines whether something survives in an adult life with a job in it.

I still have a save file from university that I open once or twice a year. It's about eleven years old at this point and I've moved it across four computers, which required actual effort on two occasions. I don't really play it any more so much as look at it — I know what every decision in it was and roughly what I was doing the week I made it. It's closer to a diary than a game at this stage, and I'd be genuinely upset to lose it, which is an odd thing to feel about a file.

So what keeps me coming back isn't the game being brilliant, though I think it is. It's that it has never once demanded my attention all at once, and at this point that's rare enough to be the whole reason.
一款策略游戏，我断断续续玩了大概十五年。不是一直在玩——我会八个月不打开它，然后连着玩三个星期。
它之所以比别的都活得久，是因为它慢到可以中途停下来。几乎没有别的游戏尊重这一点。大部分游戏都被设计成让你放下时有损失感——一局你得重来，一个你不在时还在走的计时器。这一款只是等着。我可以在一个回合中间关掉它，三月份再回来，什么都不会失去。而事实证明，在一个有工作的成年人的生活里，这一个特性决定了什么能活下来。
我大学时的存档到现在还在，每年我会打开一两次。到现在它大概十一岁了，跟着我换过四台电脑，其中有两次是真的费了力气才迁过去的。我现在与其说是在玩它，不如说是在看它——里面每一个决定我都知道是怎么回事，也大致记得做那个决定的那一周我在干什么。到这个阶段，它更像一本日记而不是一个游戏。如果丢了我会真的难受，而对一个文件产生这种感情，说起来是挺奇怪的。
所以让我一直回去的，不是这游戏有多出色，虽然我觉得它确实出色，而是它从来没有一次性要求过我全部的注意力。到了这个岁数，光这一点就足够是全部理由了。
A rabbit with one ear missing, called Tutu — which was not a considered name, it was just what a four-year-old could say.

The ear came off early, within the first year, and I'm fairly sure that's why it became the one. A toy in perfect condition is interchangeable with every other one on the shelf; a damaged one is unmistakably yours, and a child understands that instinctively even if they couldn't explain it. My mother offered to sew it back on and I refused, apparently quite forcefully, which suggests I'd already worked out that the repair would take something away.

It came with me to hospital when I was six — I had my tonsils out, nothing serious, but it was the first night I'd spent away from home. I have almost no memory of the hospital and a very clear memory of the rabbit being on the bed. It stopped being carried around when I was about nine, went into a cupboard, and moved house with my parents twice without anyone deciding it should. My mother still has it in a drawer in the spare room. I looked at it two years ago and it is much smaller and much greyer than the object in my memory, which was somehow the least surprising thing about it.

So the thing I got properly attached to was the one that was already broken. I've noticed that's held up as a pattern — I'm far more careful with things that have already been damaged than with things that are still perfect.
一只掉了一只耳朵的兔子，叫兔兔——这不是什么精心取的名字，只是一个四岁小孩能说出来的音。
那只耳朵掉得很早，第一年之内就掉了，我相当确定这正是它成为“那一只”的原因。一个完好无损的玩具和货架上其他所有玩具没有区别；一个坏掉的则明确无误地属于你，而小孩对这一点是本能地明白的，哪怕说不出来。我妈提出要把耳朵缝回去，据说我相当强烈地拒绝了，这说明我当时就已经想明白：修好它会拿走某种东西。
我六岁住院的时候是带着它去的——扁桃体手术，不是什么大事，但那是我第一次不在家里过夜。医院我几乎没有任何记忆，而兔子在床上这件事我记得非常清楚。我大概九岁的时候不再随身带着它了，它被放进柜子，后来跟着我父母搬了两次家，而没有任何人决定过它应该跟着。我妈现在还把它放在客房的抽屉里。两年前我看过一次，它比我记忆里的那个东西小得多，也灰得多，而这居然是最不让我意外的一点。
所以我真正舍不得的，是那个已经坏掉的。我发现这后来成了一种模式——对已经受过损伤的东西，我比对还完好的东西小心得多。

That if something will take under two minutes, you do it now rather than write it down. It's not original and I didn't invent it, but it's the only piece of advice I've ever taken that survived past the first fortnight.

The reason it works is that it attacks the right problem. I used to think the thing making my days feel heavy was the big items — the difficult conversation, the piece of work I was avoiding. It isn't. It's forty small things, each of which costs about ninety seconds to do and about a day and a half to carry around. Writing something on a list doesn't remove it from your head; it just adds an administrative layer to something you could have finished in the time it took to write it down.

I started applying it to email about a year ago, on the principle that if I could reply in two minutes I'd reply immediately rather than flagging it. My inbox has not gone above twenty since, and it used to sit at something like four hundred. But the effect I didn't expect was on the physical version — putting the thing away rather than on the side, replacing the light bulb when it goes rather than three weeks later. My flat is measurably tidier and I have not started being a tidier person.

So what I like about it is that it's a rule about attention rather than about effort. It doesn't ask you to do more work. It asks you to stop paying rent on work you haven't done yet, and it turns out that rent was most of what I was paying.
如果一件事两分钟之内能做完，那就现在做，别写进待办清单。这不是我想出来的，也不新鲜，但这是我采纳过的唯一一条撑过头两周的建议。
它有用的原因是它攻击的是对的问题。我以前以为让一天变得沉重的是那些大事——那场难开口的谈话、那件我一直在躲的工作。其实不是。是四十件小事，每一件做起来大概九十秒，而背在身上要背一天半。把一件事写到清单上并不能把它从你脑子里拿走，只是给一件你本可以在写它的时间里做完的事，加了一层管理成本。
我大概一年前开始把它用在邮件上，原则是：如果两分钟能回，就马上回，而不是先标记起来。从那以后我的收件箱再没超过二十封，而以前它常年在四百封左右。但我没料到的是它在实体世界的效果——东西用完直接放回去，而不是先搁在旁边；灯泡坏了当天换，而不是三个星期以后。我家明显更整齐了，而我并没有变成一个更爱整洁的人。
所以我喜欢它的地方在于，这是一条关于注意力的规则，而不是关于努力的。它不要求你做更多的事，它要求你别再为还没做的事付租金——而事实证明，我付掉的大部分就是那笔租金。
Reading in detail about things I am never going to do. Not skimming — properly reading, the way you would if there were going to be an exam, about subjects I have no intention of ever going near.

The reason I'd defend it is that almost everything else that looks like leisure has been quietly converted into self-improvement. Reading has a reading list. Exercise has a target. Even holidays get evaluated. Curiosity with no purpose attached is one of the very few things left that isn't secretly work, and I think it's genuinely restful in a way that productive hobbies are not, because there's no version of it you can fail at.

The example I always give is a Sunday I spent, about eighteen months ago, reading about how lighthouses are built. I don't know how it started — I think from a photograph. By the afternoon I understood roughly how you construct something on a rock that is underwater half the time, and I'd read a first-hand account by an engineer from the eighteen-hundreds that was genuinely gripping. I have no plans to visit a lighthouse. I have never mentioned any of this at work. Nothing came of it whatsoever, and it's one of the better Sundays I've had.

So my favourite waste of time is specifically the kind that stays wasted. The moment I start thinking a subject might be useful, it stops doing the thing I wanted it for, and I've become fairly protective of the ones that have no chance of ever being relevant.
非常仔细地读那些我这辈子都不会去做的事。不是随便扫一眼，是认真读，像要考试那样读，读的却是我根本没打算靠近的领域。
我愿意为它辩护的理由是：几乎所有看起来像休闲的东西，都已经被悄悄改造成了自我提升。读书有书单，运动有目标，连假期都要被评价。没有任何目的的好奇心，是所剩不多的、没有偷偷变成工作的东西之一。我觉得它带来的放松，是那些“有产出的爱好”给不了的，因为它没有一个你会失败的版本。
我常举的例子是大概一年半前的一个周日，我用一整天读灯塔是怎么建起来的。我已经不记得是怎么开始的了，好像是因为一张照片。到下午的时候，我大致明白了怎么在一块有一半时间泡在水下的礁石上盖东西，还读了一份十九世纪一位工程师的第一手记述，写得非常好看。我没有任何去看灯塔的计划，也从来没在工作场合提过这件事。这一整天什么都没产生，而它是我过得最好的周日之一。
所以我最喜欢的浪费时间，恰恰是那种能一直浪费下去的。只要我开始觉得某个题目“可能有用”，它就不再提供我想要的那个东西了。所以我现在相当护着那些永远都不可能派上用场的题目。
The ones to my grandparents' village, which I'd hesitate to call trips at all — nothing was booked, nothing was planned, and we did the same things every year for about eight years.

The reason they're the ones I remember is precisely that absence of a plan. A holiday with an itinerary has a shape, and a shape has an end you can see coming. Those summers had no shape at all, which made the days feel enormously long in a way I have not managed to reproduce since as an adult. I think the length was mostly boredom, honestly, and I've come round to thinking a certain amount of childhood boredom is not a problem to be solved.

We went every August for eight years and the pattern barely varied. The same walk to the same shop, the same argument about who was sleeping in which room, my grandfather doing the same thing to the same section of garden. One year it rained for six days and we played cards until we all knew each other's habits. I could describe that house room by room now, twenty years later, and I couldn't do that for any hotel I've ever stayed in.

So what made them good was the repetition, which is the exact opposite of what I now look for when I book something. There's an obvious lesson in that and I have not acted on it once — my last three holidays were all somewhere I'd never been, and I remember all three less clearly than a single August in that village.
去我祖父母村里的那些暑假。我甚至不太愿意管它们叫“旅行”——什么都没订，什么都没计划，而且连着八年做的事情几乎一模一样。
我之所以记得的是它们，恰恰是因为没有计划。有行程的假期是有形状的，而有形状就意味着你能看见结尾在靠近。那些夏天完全没有形状，于是那些日子长得不得了，而这种感觉我成年以后再也没能复制出来。老实说我觉得那份“长”里大部分其实是无聊，而我现在逐渐认为，童年里一定程度的无聊并不是一个需要被解决的问题。
我们连着八年每个八月都去，模式几乎不变：走同一条路去同一家小店，为谁睡哪个房间吵同样的架，我外公对着院子里同一块地做同样的事。有一年下了六天雨，我们打牌打到彼此的习惯都摸清了。那栋房子我现在还能一间一间地描述出来，二十年过去了；而我住过的任何一家酒店我都做不到。
所以让它们变好的是那种重复，而这恰恰和我现在订行程时追求的东西完全相反。这里面有一个很明显的教训，而我一次都没照着做过——我最近三次假期去的都是没去过的地方，而这三次加起来，我记得的都不如那个村子里的一个八月清楚。

Slow, and in one place. If you'd asked me at twenty-five I'd have described an itinerary with five cities in ten days, and I did exactly that a few times, and I came home needing a holiday from the holiday.

What changed my mind is noticing that almost nothing good happens on the second day somewhere. The second day is admin — finding the shop, working out the bus, discovering which café is actually good rather than merely nearest. If you leave on the third morning you've paid all of that cost and collected none of the return. Staying put means you get the version of a place that only exists once you've stopped being a visitor to it.

The trip that proved it was two summers ago. We rented a flat in one small town for ten days and did almost nothing that would look good written down. We went to the same café every morning — by day four the woman behind the counter had our order ready — and we swam at the same beach, and twice we didn't leave the flat until noon. On the last evening a neighbour we'd said hello to all week invited us in for a drink, which would never have happened on day two. I came home genuinely rested for the first time in years.

So the way I judge a holiday now is almost embarrassingly simple: how many times did I open and close the suitcase? One is ideal. Anything above three and I know I've booked a trip rather than a rest.
慢一点，而且待在一个地方。如果你二十五岁的时候问我，我会给你描述一个十天五个城市的行程，我也确实那样玩过几次，结果每次回来都需要再放一次假。
让我改变想法的，是我发现到了一个地方的第二天几乎不会发生什么好事。第二天全是杂事——找超市、研究公交、弄清楚哪家咖啡馆是真的好，而不只是最近。如果第三天早上就走，你把这些成本都付了，却一点回报都没拿到。待着不动，你才能看到一个地方在你不再是“游客”之后的样子。
证明这一点的是前年夏天那次。我们在一个小城租了十天的公寓，做的事情几乎没有一件写下来好看的。我们每天早上去同一家咖啡馆——到第四天，柜台后面那位女士已经提前把我们要的准备好了；我们在同一片海滩游泳；有两天我们中午之前根本没出门。最后一天晚上，一个我们打了一星期招呼的邻居请我们进去喝了一杯，这种事在第二天是绝不可能发生的。那次回家，是我多年来第一次真的休息过了。
所以我现在判断一次假期好不好的标准简单得有点不好意思：我一共开合了几次行李箱？一次最理想。超过三次，我就知道自己订的是一次行程，而不是一次休息。

One younger brother, four years between us. For most of my childhood I'd have described that as an unfortunate arrangement, and I'd now say it was the single luckiest structural fact of my upbringing.

The four-year gap is the reason. It was wide enough that we were never competing for the same thing at the same time — different schools, different friends, never the same teacher comparing us. I've watched siblings eighteen months apart go through their entire childhood being measured against each other, and I don't think either of them chose that. We were spared it entirely by an accident of timing, and I've never fully lost the sense that we got away with something.

That said, we fought more or less continuously until I left home at eighteen — over the television, over him coming into my room, over nothing that either of us could reconstruct now. What changed it was distance. I moved away, and for about a year we barely spoke, and then somewhere around the second Christmas we started having actual conversations rather than the exchange of information that had passed for it before. He's now the person I call when something has gone wrong, which is not a sentence twenty-year-old me would have believed.

So we get on far better as adults than we ever did as children, and I've come to think that's the normal shape rather than a happy exception. You're not really friends with somebody you're forced to share a bathroom with. You can only find out whether you like each other once nobody has to be there.
一个弟弟，我们差四岁。我童年的大部分时间都会说这是个不幸的安排，而我现在会说，这是我成长过程中最幸运的一个结构性事实。
关键就是这四岁的差距。它大到我们从来不会在同一时间争同一样东西——不同的学校、不同的朋友，也从来没有同一个老师拿我们作比较。我见过差一岁半的兄弟姐妹，整个童年都在被互相衡量，而我不觉得那是他们两个谁选的。我们纯粹因为时间上的巧合完全躲开了这件事，我到现在都还有一种“我们侥幸逃掉了什么”的感觉。
话虽如此，在我十八岁离开家之前，我们几乎是一直在吵——为了电视，为了他进我房间，为了那些我们现在谁都还原不出来的事。改变这一切的是距离。我搬走以后，有大概一年我们几乎不说话；然后大概在第二个春节前后，我们开始有了真正的对话，而不是之前那种当作对话的信息交换。他现在是我出事时第一个会打电话的人，而这句话，二十岁的我是不会相信的。
所以我们成年以后的关系比小时候好太多了，而我逐渐觉得这才是正常的形状，不是什么幸运的例外。你和一个被迫跟你共用一个卫生间的人，其实算不上朋友。只有在谁都不必待在那里之后，你们才有机会发现彼此喜不喜欢对方。
Less than I used to, and I've become quite specific about why. I read a great many in my twenties and I'd now rather read a good biography of the same person by somebody else.

The reason is structural rather than about any particular book. An autobiography is written by the one person least able to see the shape of the story, because they were inside it and because they have to live with the consequences of what they say. Every person still alive in the book is somebody the author will have to face. That doesn't make them dishonest, but it means the interesting questions — what did this cost other people, what were they wrong about — are precisely the ones the form is worst at.

I read two last year by people I genuinely admire, and by the end of both I felt I understood a great deal about how they wished to be seen and very little about what had actually happened. One of them had an early failure that had clearly mattered enormously, and it got a page and a half, positioned so that it read as the beginning of the recovery. A biographer would have spent a chapter there. I've since read a biography of a different figure that was openly unsure about its subject's motives in two places, and I trusted it far more for saying so.

So my position is that autobiography is the best possible source for what somebody believes about themselves and a fairly poor one for anything else. I still read them — I just read them now as evidence rather than as an account.
比以前喜欢得少，而且我现在能说得很具体。我二十多岁的时候读过很多自传，现在我更愿意读别人写的、关于同一个人的好传记。
原因是结构性的，跟具体哪本书无关。自传是由最看不清这个故事形状的那个人写的，因为他就在故事里面，而且他要承担自己所说内容的后果。书里每一个还活着的人，都是作者以后还要面对的人。这不代表他们不诚实，但这意味着那些真正有意思的问题——这件事让别人付出了什么代价、他们在哪里错了——恰恰是这种体裁最不擅长回答的。
去年我读了两本，作者都是我真心敬佩的人。读完之后我觉得，我非常了解他们希望别人怎么看他们，却几乎不了解当时到底发生了什么。其中一位早年有一次明显影响巨大的失败，在书里只占了一页半，而且位置安排得让它读起来像是“重新振作的开始”。一个传记作者会在那里写一整章。后来我读了一本写别人的传记，作者在两处坦白说自己也拿不准传主的动机，而我因为这份坦白反而更信任它。
所以我的立场是：自传是了解一个人如何看待自己的最好材料，而对别的事情来说是相当差的材料。我还是会读，只是现在把它们当作证据来读，而不是当作叙述。
I like the first day of it enormously and I dislike every day after it, and I've stopped pretending that's a contradiction because it clearly isn't.

The two things being judged are completely different. Day one is a visual event — everything familiar looks unfamiliar, sound behaves oddly, and there's a genuine and slightly childish pleasure in that which I don't think I'll ever lose. Day three is a logistics problem. The snow is grey, the pavement is ice, and the same substance that was beautiful on Saturday is now the reason a twelve-minute walk takes twenty-five and involves concentrating on the ground the whole way.

Last February made the point precisely. It came down heavily on a Saturday, which is the best possible timing, and I spent about an hour outside for no reason at all, which I hadn't done in months. By Tuesday I'd fallen over twice on the way to work — properly fallen, not stumbled — and I was calculating routes based on which streets faced the sun. The same snow. Nothing about it had changed except that I now had somewhere to be.

So my feelings about snow turn out to be almost entirely a function of whether I have an obligation that day. On a Saturday it's the best weather there is. On a Wednesday it's the worst, and I think most people who say they love snow are quietly describing the Saturday version.
下雪的第一天我非常喜欢，之后的每一天都不喜欢。我已经不再假装这是个矛盾了，因为它显然不是。
被评价的其实是两件完全不同的东西。第一天是一个视觉事件——所有熟悉的东西都变得陌生，声音的传播方式也变得奇怪，那里面有一种真实的、略带孩子气的快乐，我想我这辈子都不会失去。第三天则是一个交通问题：雪是灰的，人行道是冰，周六还很美的同一样东西，现在成了十二分钟的路要走二十五分钟、而且全程都得盯着地面的原因。
去年二月把这一点说得很清楚。雪是周六下的，这是最理想的时机，我毫无理由地在外面待了大概一个小时，而这种事我已经几个月没做过了。到周二，我在上班路上摔了两次——是真摔，不是踉跄——而且我开始按“哪条街朝阳”来规划路线。同样的雪，除了我现在有地方非去不可以外，什么都没变。
所以我对雪的感觉，几乎完全取决于那天我有没有非做不可的事。周六它是最好的天气，周三它是最糟的。而我觉得，大部分说自己爱雪的人，其实说的都是周六那个版本。
Dogs, all through my childhood, and always two at a time — never one. That wasn't an accident, it was a policy my parents had and defended.

The reasoning was my mother's: she believed a dog on its own is bored and a bored dog is a badly behaved one, and she'd rather do twice the walking than deal with the alternative. Whether that's true I genuinely don't know, but it shaped what having animals felt like in our house. Two dogs are not one dog twice — they're a small society that mostly entertains itself, and the house was never quiet in a way I only appreciated after I'd left it.

For about ten years there were always two of them moving around the place, usually within a metre of each other. When the first one died the second one changed noticeably — slower, more attached to my mother, needing to be in whichever room people were. And when she went too, about eighteen months later, the house was genuinely startling. I remember coming home that Christmas and the silence being the first thing I noticed at the door, before I'd taken my coat off. My parents haven't had a dog since and I don't think they will.

So what having pets means to me isn't companionship in the one-to-one sense people usually describe. It's noise, and movement, and the fact that a house with animals in it is never entirely still — and I notice I still find completely quiet houses slightly wrong.
养狗，整个童年都在养，而且永远是同时养两只，从来不只养一只。这不是偶然，是我父母的一条政策，而且他们会为它辩护。
理由是我妈的：她认为一只狗单独待着会无聊，而无聊的狗行为就会变坏，她宁愿多遛一倍的路，也不想应付那个后果。这话对不对我是真不知道，但它塑造了我们家养动物的感觉。两只狗不等于一只狗乘以二——它们是一个小社会，大部分时候自己就把自己逗开心了。我们家从来不安静，而这一点我是离开家以后才体会到的。
有差不多十年，家里总是有两只在走来走去，通常互相不超过一米。第一只走了以后，第二只明显变了——变慢了，更黏我妈，一定要待在有人的那个房间里。大概一年半以后她也走了，那时候房子安静得让人吃惊。我记得那年过年回家，我在门口还没脱外套，第一个注意到的就是那份安静。我父母从那以后再没养过狗，我想他们也不会了。
所以对我来说，养宠物的意义不是大家通常说的那种一对一的陪伴，而是声音、是动静，是一个有动物的家从来不会完全静止。我发现直到现在，我还是觉得完全安静的房子有点不对劲。
Card games, almost entirely, and I think the reason is much more practical than it sounds — they were the ones that could go anywhere.

A board game requires a table, a flat surface, forty minutes of setup tolerance and everybody agreeing to commit. A deck of cards works on a train, on a floor, in a power cut, in a car if you're careful, and in the twenty minutes before something else happens. That flexibility means the card games got played hundreds of times and the board games got played at Christmas. Repetition is what turns a game into a shared reference, and only one of those categories got enough of it.

The specific one is a game my family has played every Christmas for as long as I can remember. The rules are simple, the game is largely luck, and none of that matters because what's actually happening is four people insulting each other for two hours in a way that's only permitted during the game. My father cheats. He has always cheated, everybody knows, and his cheating is now so thoroughly part of the tradition that the year he played straight — because he was ill — it wasn't as good. My mother keeps score in the same notebook, and there are years in it from before I was born.

So the games that stuck were the ones that needed nothing but people. Everything else needed the right conditions, and the right conditions turn out to be rare enough that they never accumulated into anything.
几乎全是纸牌类的。我觉得原因比听起来实际得多——因为它们是能带到任何地方去的那一类。
桌游需要一张桌子、一个平面、四十分钟布置的耐心，还需要所有人都同意投入进去。而一副牌在火车上能玩、在地板上能玩、停电时能玩、小心一点在车里也能玩，在“离下一件事还有二十分钟”的空档里也能玩。这种灵活性意味着纸牌被玩了几百次，而桌游只在过年时被玩。是重复把一个游戏变成一个共同的暗号，而这两类里只有一类得到了足够的重复。
具体的那一个，是我们家从我记事起每年过年都会玩的一种牌。规则很简单，胜负基本靠运气，而这些都不重要，因为真正在发生的事是四个人用一种只有在牌局里才被允许的方式互相挖苦两个小时。我爸耍赖。他一直都耍赖，所有人都知道，而他的耍赖现在已经彻底成了这个传统的一部分——有一年他因为生病规规矩矩地打，那一年反而没那么好玩。我妈用同一个本子记分，那本子里有些年份比我出生还早。
所以留下来的游戏，都是除了人什么都不需要的那种。别的都需要合适的条件，而合适的条件稀有到它们从来没有累积成什么东西。
A factory town I had never heard of before I was told I was going there, and would struggle to place on a map even now if you took the label off.

What made it interesting is precisely that nothing about it had been arranged for visitors. There was no old quarter, no restaurant anyone would recommend, no view. Which meant that everything I saw was the place doing what it actually does, rather than a version of itself assembled for people passing through. I've been to genuinely beautiful cities for work and remembered almost nothing, because a hotel and a conference room look the same everywhere.

I was there four days and I ate every meal in the same canteen as everyone else, mostly because there wasn't an alternative. That turned out to be the whole trip. You learn more about how an organisation works from what people complain about over lunch than from anything said in a meeting, and by day three two people were telling me things that would never have made it into a formal conversation. I also got shown a machine somebody's father had helped install thirty years earlier, which was mentioned in passing and was clearly a point of pride.

So the trips I actually remember are the ones where nobody was showing me anything. Being deliberately hosted is pleasant and it's also a filter, and I've started asking to eat where people eat rather than where visitors are taken.
一个我被通知要去之前完全没听说过的工业城市。哪怕现在，如果你把地名遮住，我大概也很难在地图上指出来。
让它有意思的地方，恰恰是那里没有任何东西是为了接待外来者而准备的。没有老城区，没有谁会推荐的餐馆，也没有什么景色。这意味着我看到的每一样东西，都是这个地方在做它本来在做的事，而不是它为路过的人拼出来的一个版本。我因为工作去过真正漂亮的城市，却几乎什么都没记住，因为酒店和会议室在哪里都长一个样。
我在那儿待了四天，每顿饭都和当地人在同一个食堂吃，主要是因为没有别的选择。结果那才是整趟出差的全部。你从午饭时别人抱怨的内容里，能了解到的关于一个机构如何运转的东西，比会上说的任何话都多。到第三天，有两个人开始跟我说一些绝不可能出现在正式场合的事。还有人带我看了一台机器，是他父亲三十年前参与安装的——这件事是顺口提起的，但那种自豪很明显。
所以我真正记住的出差，都是没有人特意带我参观的那几次。被刻意招待当然舒服，但它同时也是一层过滤。我现在开始主动要求去当地人吃饭的地方，而不是接待客人的地方。
I say yes when it's genuinely urgent and I say no, plainly, when it isn't. That sounds obvious but it took me about five years to be able to do it without a long apologetic explanation attached.

The reason I stopped agreeing to everything is that saying yes automatically doesn't read as helpfulness — it reads as availability. If your evenings are free by default, the requests will expand to fill them, not because anyone is being unreasonable but because you've quietly told them there's no cost. I also noticed the work I did at nine at night was measurably worse, so I was trading good hours tomorrow for bad hours tonight and calling it commitment.

There was a stretch last spring where I stayed late every week for about two months. What broke the pattern wasn't a confrontation — it was one question I started asking, which is simply: what happens if this waits until tomorrow morning? About two-thirds of the time the honest answer turned out to be nothing at all, and once I'd asked it a few times the requests themselves started arriving pre-filtered. My manager, to be fair to her, never once pushed back on it. I think she'd had no idea how many of those requests were being passed along unexamined.

So my rule now is that I'm not protecting my evenings on principle. I'm asking for the deadline to be real. If it is, I'll stay as late as it takes, and I've done that twice this year without resenting a minute of it.
如果确实紧急我会答应，如果不是，我会直接说不。这听起来理所当然，但我花了大概五年，才能做到说不的时候不附带一长串道歉式的解释。
我不再什么都答应的原因是：习惯性地说好，别人读到的不是“乐于助人”，而是“随时有空”。如果你的晚上默认是空的，这类要求就会一直扩张到把它填满——不是因为谁在为难你，而是因为你已经悄悄告诉了他们这没有成本。我还发现，我晚上九点做的活儿明显更差，所以我其实是在用明天状态好的几个小时，换今晚状态差的几个小时，然后把这叫作敬业。
去年春天有大概两个月，我每周都加班。打破这个循环的不是一次正面冲突，而是我开始问的一个问题：如果这件事等到明天早上会怎么样？大概有三分之二的时候，老实的答案是什么都不会怎么样。而我问了几次之后，送到我这里的要求本身就开始被提前筛过一遍了。公平地说，我的主管一次都没有反对过。我想她此前根本不知道，有多少这样的要求是没经过判断就往下传的。
所以我现在的原则不是出于立场保住晚上，而是要求那个截止时间是真的。如果它是真的，需要多晚我就待多晚——今年我这样做过两次，一分钟都没有不情愿。
How much of it is decided by a calendar rather than by me. Not any particular commitment — each one is defensible on its own — but the aggregate, which nobody ever agreed to.

The mechanism is what bothers me. Nothing in my week arrived by a decision I'd recognise as a decision. Each item was a reasonable thing to say yes to at the moment I was asked, usually weeks in advance, when the day it landed on looked pleasantly empty. The result is that my life is largely being run by a version of me from three weeks ago who was being generous with somebody else's time, and who is, structurally, incapable of learning from the experience.

I noticed the scale of it last month. I went back through the previous four weeks and counted the evenings with nothing in them at all, and the answer was three out of twenty-eight. That's not a busy period, that's just what my calendar looks like now, and none of it is work — it's dinners and favours and things I genuinely wanted to go to when I agreed. Two of those three empty evenings I spent doing admin I'd been putting off, so really it was one.

So what I'd change isn't any single thing on the list. It's the moment of agreeing, which currently costs me nothing and should cost something. I've started saying I'll check and reply tomorrow, which sounds trivial, but it puts a small amount of friction in exactly the place where there wasn't any.
我的生活有太多是由日程表决定的，而不是我自己决定的。不是某一件具体的安排——每一件单独拿出来都说得通——而是它们加在一起的总量，而那个总量从来没有人同意过。
让我在意的是这个机制。我一周里的任何一件事，都不是通过一个我会认作“决定”的决定来到我这里的。每一件在被问到的当下都是合理的、值得答应的，而且通常是提前好几周问的，那时候它落到的那一天看起来空得很舒服。结果就是，我的生活很大程度上是被三个星期前那个版本的我在管理——那个版本正在慷慨地支配别人的时间，而且从结构上讲，他永远学不到教训。
上个月我才意识到这件事的规模。我回头数了前面四个星期里完全没有安排的晚上，答案是二十八天里只有三个。那还不是什么特别忙的时期，那就是我的日程表现在的样子。而且这些安排都不是工作——是聚餐、是帮忙、是我答应的时候真心想去的事。那三个空出来的晚上里，有两个我用来处理一直拖着的杂事，所以其实只有一个。
所以我想改的不是清单上的任何一项，而是“答应”的那一刻——它目前对我毫无成本，而它应该有成本。我现在开始说“我看一下，明天回复你”。这听起来微不足道，但它恰恰在原本一点摩擦都没有的地方，加进了一点摩擦。
The corner of the sofa closest to the window. It's a specific corner, not a general preference, and everybody in the house knows it.

The reason is that it's the only seat in the flat that solves two things at once — I can see out of the window, and I can still hear whoever is in the kitchen. Every other position gives you one or the other. The armchair has a better view and is acoustically cut off; the chair at the table is in the conversation but faces a wall. That corner is the only place where I can be doing my own thing and still be present, and it turns out that's the state I want to be in most of the time.

It's become slightly ridiculous. Everyone in the house leaves it empty — not because I've asked, but because the third or fourth time somebody sits there and I visibly hover, a convention forms. My partner refers to it as my office. When we had people over at New Year somebody sat in it for about two hours and I noticed I was mildly, unreasonably annoyed the entire time, which told me more about myself than I wanted to know.
So it's less a favourite seat than an agreed one, and I think most households have two or three of these. Nobody negotiates them, nobody writes them down, and everyone knows exactly where they are.
靠窗那一角的沙发。是特定的那一角，不是笼统的偏好，而且家里所有人都知道。
原因是，那是整个房子里唯一一个能同时解决两件事的位置——我既能看见窗外，又能听见厨房里的人说话。其他任何位置都只能给你其中一个：扶手椅视野更好，但声音上是断开的；餐桌旁的椅子在谈话里，但面对着一面墙。那个角落是唯一一个我可以做自己的事、同时又在场的地方，而事实证明，那是我大部分时候想处在的状态。
这件事已经有点荒唐了。家里人都会把那个位置空出来——不是因为我要求过，而是因为第三次或第四次有人坐在那儿、我明显在旁边转悠之后，一个惯例就形成了。我的伴侣管它叫我的办公室。过年家里来客人的时候，有个人在那儿坐了大概两个小时，我发现自己全程都有点没道理地不痛快，这件事让我对自己的了解超出了我想知道的程度。
所以与其说那是我最喜欢的座位，不如说是大家默认的座位。我觉得大多数家庭都有两三个这样的位置：没人谈判过，没人写下来，但每个人都清楚它们在哪儿。
That they haven't yet learned to pretend to be interested. It's the quality I'd most like to keep some version of, and the one that gets trained out of everybody by about eleven.

The reason I value it is that adult conversation runs almost entirely on a polite fiction. We nod through things we don't care about, and we do it so automatically that we often can't tell whether the person opposite is engaged or performing, and neither can they. A child gives you completely reliable information. If they're still there, they're interested. If they've left, they're not. You can calibrate against that in a way you never can with an adult.

The clearest demonstration was my niece, who is seven, asking me what my job was. I gave what I thought was a reasonably good simplified answer. She listened for about ten seconds, said 'that sounds boring' with no malice whatsoever, and walked out of the room. My sister apologised. I genuinely didn't need her to — it was the most accurate feedback I'd had on how I describe my work in about a decade, and I've since changed how I answer that question at parties.

So what I like is the honesty, including when it's at my expense. I don't think children are wiser than adults about very much, but on the specific question of whether something is actually interesting they are the only reliable instrument available.
他们还没学会假装感兴趣。这是我最希望自己能保留下某个版本的品质，也是所有人在十一岁左右就被训练掉的那一个。
我看重它的原因是：成年人的对话几乎完全建立在一种礼貌的虚构之上。我们会对自己并不在意的事点头，而且做得如此自动，以至于我们常常分不清对面的人是投入还是在表演——他们自己往往也分不清。而小孩给你的信息是完全可靠的：他还在，就是有兴趣；他走了，就是没有。你可以拿这个来校准自己，而对着成年人你永远做不到。
最清楚的一次是我七岁的侄女问我做什么工作。我给了一个自认为还算不错的简化版回答。她听了大概十秒，说了句“听起来好无聊”，语气里没有任何恶意，然后就走出了房间。我姐姐替她道歉。我是真的不需要——那是我大概十年来收到过的、关于“我怎么描述自己的工作”最准确的反馈。从那以后，我在聚会上回答这个问题的方式就改了。
所以我喜欢的是那种诚实，包括被说的是我自己的时候。我不觉得小孩在很多事情上比大人更有智慧，但在“某样东西到底有没有意思”这个具体问题上，他们是唯一可靠的仪器。
I go outside and walk, and the important part is that I do it specifically when I don't feel like it. The days I want to go for a walk aren't the days that need one.

The reason it works, as far as I can tell, is that a bad mood indoors has nothing to push against. You sit with it, and it fills the available space, and after two hours it's stopped being about whatever started it and has become a general position about your life. Moving interrupts that. I don't think it's really about exercise or fresh air or any of the things people say — it's that the scenery changes every few seconds and a mood needs a stable environment to grow in.

The clearest test I've run on this was last winter, during a fairly grim few weeks. I made myself walk for twenty minutes every evening — not a long walk, not a scenic one, just around the same three streets in the dark and the cold. The first three days I resented every minute. By Wednesday of the second week I noticed I was going out slightly earlier than I had to. By Friday I felt noticeably better, and I don't think anything in my circumstances had changed at all. That's what convinced me it wasn't a solution to the problem so much as a way of stopping the problem being the only thing in the room.
So my honest answer is that I don't try to cheer myself up, because I've never once managed it by deciding to. I change where I am, and the mood usually follows within about a quarter of an hour.
我会出门走走，而关键的部分是：我专门在不想动的时候去走。想去散步的那些日子，恰恰是不需要散步的日子。
据我观察，它之所以有用，是因为坏心情待在屋里没有任何东西可以顶着它。你陪着它坐，它就把可用的空间全填满，两个小时以后，它已经不是关于最初那件事了，而变成了关于你整个人生的一个结论。动起来会打断这个过程。我觉得这跟运动或者新鲜空气其实关系不大——而是外面的景象每几秒就变一次，而一种情绪需要一个稳定的环境才能长大。
我做过的最清楚的一次验证是去年冬天，那几周过得相当糟。我逼自己每天晚上走二十分钟——不是长距离，也不是什么风景，就是在黑暗和寒冷里绕同样的三条街。头三天我每一分钟都不情愿。到第二周的星期三，我发现自己出门的时间比必须出门的时间稍微早了一点。到星期五我明显感觉好多了，而我的处境其实一点都没变。就是这一点让我确信，它不是问题的解决方案，而是一种让问题不再是房间里唯一那件事的方法。
所以我真实的回答是：我不试图让自己开心起来，因为我从来没有靠“决定开心”成功过一次。我改变自己所在的位置，心情通常会在一刻钟之内跟上来。
Yes, though it was a much closer thing than it sounds, and I applied a year later than everybody I'd been at school with.

The reason it wasn't obvious is that nobody in my family had been, so there was no assumption in the house that this was what happened next. It wasn't discouraged — my parents were entirely supportive — but the default option in front of me was to start earning, and that had a clarity to it that three more years of not earning did not. When you're eighteen and don't know anyone who's done a thing, that thing doesn't feel like a decision so much as a departure.

So I worked for twelve months first, in a job I was reasonably good at and could see the whole of within about five weeks. That year is the reason the degree meant anything. I've watched people go straight through and treat the first year as an extension of school, and I understand it completely, because without the twelve months I'd have done exactly the same. I went in knowing precisely what the alternative looked like, which turns out to be the most useful thing you can know when you're deciding whether to bother turning up to something at nine in the morning.

So I'm glad I went, and I'm gladder I went late. If I were advising somebody in the same position I wouldn't tell them to take a year off, exactly — I'd tell them to spend a year doing something they can see the end of.
上了，不过比听起来要悬得多，而且我比中学同学晚了一年才申请。
之所以不是理所当然，是因为我们家没有人上过大学，所以家里并没有“接下来就该这样”的默认设定。这不是说有人劝阻——我父母完全支持——而是摆在我面前的默认选项是去挣钱，而那件事有一种清晰感，是“再有三年不挣钱”所没有的。当你十八岁，身边没有一个人做过某件事时，那件事感觉上不像一个决定，更像一次离开。
所以我先工作了十二个月，做的是一份我还算擅长、而且大概五个星期就能看到全貌的工作。正是那一年，让后来的学位有了意义。我见过直接升上去的人，把大一当成中学的延长，我完全理解，因为没有那十二个月，我做的会一模一样。我是清清楚楚地知道另一条路长什么样才进去的，而事实证明，当你要决定值不值得早上九点爬起来去上课时，这是最有用的一项信息。
所以我很庆幸自己去了，更庆幸去得晚。如果要我给处在同样位置的人建议，我不会正好说“休学一年”——我会说：花一年去做一件你能看见它尽头的事。
Mostly by agreeing to do things I can't do yet, in front of people who will notice if I do them badly. Which is an uncomfortable answer, but every alternative I've tried has quietly failed.

The reason courses never worked for me is that nothing depends on them. I've started six or seven and finished one. There's no consequence to stopping in week three, so week three is where I stop, and I've stopped blaming my discipline for that because the pattern is far too consistent to be personal. Being responsible for something, on the other hand, has never once failed to make me learn it, because the deadline belongs to somebody else and embarrassment is a much more reliable motivator than curiosity.

The clearest case was about two years ago, when the person who made our team's presentations left and nobody replaced her. I volunteered, mostly because the alternative was worse slides. For three months I made things that were genuinely bad and got told so, politely, most weeks. I learned more about how information should be laid out in that period than in the two books on the subject I'd read beforehand and remembered nothing from. The difference is that the books had no Thursday in them.

So my method now is deliberately to look for the thing I'm not qualified for and put my hand up early, while the stakes are still low enough that being bad at it is survivable. It's not comfortable, but at this point I've stopped expecting learning to be.
主要是靠答应去做那些我还不会的事，而且是在会注意到我做得不好的人面前做。这个答案不太舒服，但我试过的所有别的方法都悄悄失败了。
上课对我从来没用，原因是没有任何东西依赖它。我开始过六七门课，只学完过一门。第三周停下来没有任何后果，所以第三周就是我停下来的地方。我已经不再怪自己意志力差了，因为这个规律太一致了，不像是个人问题。反过来，只要我要为某件事负责，就没有一次不学会的，因为那个截止时间是别人的，而尴尬这个动力，比好奇心可靠得多。
最清楚的一次是大概两年前，我们组做幻灯片的那个人离职了，也没人接替。我主动接了下来，主要是因为不接的话幻灯片会更难看。有三个月我做出来的东西是真的很差，而且几乎每周都会有人客气地告诉我。那段时间我学到的关于“信息该怎么排布”的东西，比我之前读过的两本相关的书多得多——那两本书我一点都没记住。区别在于，书里没有星期四。
所以我现在的方法是刻意去找那些我还不够格的事，趁着风险还小、做得差还能承受的时候早点举手。这不舒服，但到了这个阶段，我已经不指望学习是舒服的了。
She told me what she actually thought, which sounds like a low bar and turned out to be something I'd never had before or since in quite the same form.

The reason it mattered so much is that most managers I've worked for were kind in a way that left me guessing. Nothing was ever wrong exactly, feedback arrived wrapped in enough qualification to be deniable, and I spent a lot of energy trying to work out where I actually stood from tone of voice and how quickly emails came back. That's an exhausting way to work, and the worst part is that it looks like a good relationship from the outside.

The moment I always come back to was in my first month. I'd produced something I was reasonably pleased with and she said, without any preamble, that it wasn't good enough yet. I remember the physical sensation. And then — this is the part that matters — she sat down for forty minutes and went through why, section by section, and at the end I understood something about the work I hadn't understood that morning. If she'd only done the first half I'd have remembered her as harsh. If she'd only done the second I'd have learned less. She did both, and she did both every time for two years.

So what made her good wasn't the willingness to criticise, which is common enough and often just self-indulgence. It was that she stayed in the room for the second part, and I've since noticed how rarely those two things travel together.
她会直接告诉我她真正的想法。这听起来门槛很低，但事实证明，这是我此前和此后都没有以完全相同的形式得到过的东西。
它之所以那么重要，是因为我共事过的大部分主管都很客气，客气到让我一直在猜。什么都算不上不对，反馈总是被包裹在足够多的限定词里，随时可以被否认，而我要花很大力气从语气和回邮件的快慢里推断自己到底处在什么位置。那是一种极其消耗的工作方式，而最糟的是，从外面看它像是一段很好的关系。
我总会想起入职第一个月的那一刻。我交了一份自己还算满意的东西，她没有任何铺垫，直接说这还不够好。那种身体上的感觉我到现在还记得。然后——这才是关键的部分——她坐下来，用了四十分钟，一段一段地讲为什么。等她讲完，我明白了一些那天早上还不明白的事。如果她只做了前半部分，我记住的会是一个严厉的人；如果她只做了后半部分，我学到的会少得多。她两件都做了，而且两年里每一次都两件都做。
所以她好的地方不在于愿意批评——那其实很常见，而且常常只是自我满足——而在于她为了后半部分留在了房间里。我后来才注意到，这两件事同时出现的概率有多低。
