The problem-solving, and I'd say that's true regardless of what the job is called. I've had the title change three times in six years and the part I enjoy has been identical throughout.

The reason is that I need to be able to point at something at the end of a day and say that it is different because I was there. A lot of office work fails that test — you attend, you contribute, you go home, and if you'd been ill that day the outcome would have been broadly the same. That's not a complaint about anyone, it's just how a lot of coordinating work is shaped. But it means the days I actually feel good about are the days where something was broken and now isn't.

The clearest recent example was a fortnight ago. There was a report the whole team had to produce every Monday, and it took about three hours because the data came out of two systems that disagreed about how to name things. Everybody complained about it and nobody fixed it, for the very ordinary reason that fixing it wasn't anyone's job. I spent two days on it and now it takes about ten minutes. Nine people got roughly two and a half hours of their week back permanently. Honestly, that felt better than the promotion I got last year, and I've thought about why ever since.
So what keeps me in a job isn't the direction it's heading in. It's whether the work itself has that shape — a before and an after, where the after is better and I can see my hand in it.
解决问题的过程，而且我觉得不管这份工作叫什么名字，这一点都成立。六年里我的职位换过三次，我享受的那部分一直没变。
原因是，我需要在一天结束的时候能指着某样东西说：这里因为我而不同。很多办公室工作过不了这一关——你出席、你发言、你回家，而如果那天你请了病假，结果大概也差不多。这不是在抱怨谁，很多协调性的工作本来就是这个形状。但这意味着，让我真正觉得好的日子，是那种“有东西坏了，现在不坏了”的日子。
最近最清楚的例子是两个星期前。我们组每周一都要出一份报告，要花大概三个小时，因为数据来自两个系统，而这两个系统对同一样东西的命名方式不一致。所有人都抱怨，但没有人去修，理由很平常：修它不是任何一个人的职责。我花了两天，现在这份报告十分钟就能出。九个人从此每周永久多出大约两个半小时。老实说，那种感觉比我去年升职还好，而我从那以后一直在想为什么。
所以让我留在一份工作里的，不是它通向哪里，而是这份工作本身有没有那个形状：有一个之前，有一个之后，之后更好，而且我能看见自己在里面的那只手。
University, and it isn't close — I'd say the gap is about as wide as it could be without me having actively disliked school, which I didn't.

The reason is straightforward: school was something that happened to me and university was the first thing I chose. I didn't pick the school, or the subjects for most of it, or the people I spent every day with. That's not a criticism, it's just what being fifteen is. But it means my memories of it are mostly of managing a situation rather than building one, and there's a limit to how fondly you can look back on a situation you were managing.

The concrete difference was the first fortnight. I met three of the people I'm still closest to inside two weeks, essentially at random — one because of where we were both standing during a queue, one because we'd chosen the same optional module out of nine. All three are still in my life fifteen years later; two were at my thirtieth. In seven years of school I made one friendship that survived, and I saw those people every day for far longer.

So what I remember more fondly is the period where the decisions were mine, including the bad ones. I think that's what people are actually describing when they say university was the best time of their life — not the freedom in the general sense, but the first stretch where the shape of a week was something you'd assembled rather than been handed.
大学，而且差得不是一点半点。我会说，这个差距已经大到不能再大了，前提是我并不讨厌中学——我确实不讨厌。
原因很直接：中学是发生在我身上的事，大学是我第一次自己做的选择。学校不是我挑的，大部分科目不是我挑的，每天朝夕相处的人也不是我挑的。这不是批评，十五岁本来就是这样。但这意味着我对中学的记忆，大多是在“应付一个局面”，而不是在“搭建一个局面”，而一个你只是在应付的局面，能被怀念的程度是有上限的。
具体的区别体现在开学头两个星期。我在两周之内认识了三个到现在还最要好的人，基本上都是随机的——一个是因为排队时我们俩站的位置，一个是因为我们在九门选修课里选了同一门。十五年过去，这三个人都还在我的生活里，其中两个来参加了我的三十岁生日。而在七年的中学生活里，我只交下了一个撑到今天的朋友，而那些人我每天见，见的时间长得多。
所以我更怀念的，是那段决定由我自己做的日子，包括那些做错的决定。我觉得大家说“大学是人生最好的时光”时，真正在描述的就是这个——不是笼统意义上的自由，而是人生中第一段“一周的形状是你自己拼出来的、而不是别人递给你的”时间。

I sort them, reasonably carefully, while being genuinely unsure a fair amount of the time whether I'm doing it right. Both halves of that sentence are true and I've stopped feeling bad about the second one.

The reason for the uncertainty isn't laziness. The rules where I live have changed twice in five years, and the second change was communicated by a leaflet that arrived while I was away and a sticker on a bin that had already faded. Nobody has ever explained what happens to any of it. So you end up doing a slightly anxious version of the right thing, based on a mixture of the old rules, the new ones, and what your neighbours appear to be doing.

In practice I keep three bins in the kitchen, which is one more than the flat has room for, and I still find myself looking things up on my phone about once a week. Coffee cups took me two years to get right — they look like paper and are not. Anything with a film on it, anything with food residue, anything that's two materials stuck together: those are the cases where I still guess. I asked at the council office once and got an answer that contradicted the leaflet.

So I'd say I try, and the system makes trying much harder than it needs to be. If the rules were on the bin in the same words every year I suspect the average household would get this right without any effort at all, and I don't think the difficulty is doing anybody any good.
我会分类，而且分得还算仔细，同时相当多的时候确实不确定自己分得对不对。这句话的两半都是真的，而我已经不再为后半句感到愧疚了。
不确定的原因不是懒。我们这边的规定五年里改了两次，第二次改的时候，通知方式是一张我不在家时送来的传单，加上一张贴在垃圾桶上、当时就已经褪色的贴纸。也从来没有人解释过这些东西最后去了哪里。于是你只能做一个略带焦虑版本的“正确的事”，依据是旧规定、新规定，以及邻居看起来在怎么做，这三者的混合。
实际操作上，我厨房里放了三个垃圾桶，比这个厨房容得下的多一个，而我还是大概每周都要拿手机查一次。咖啡杯我花了两年才弄对——它们看起来是纸，其实不是。表面有一层膜的、沾了食物残渣的、两种材料粘在一起的：这些情况我到现在还是靠猜。我去街道办问过一次，得到的答案和传单上的是矛盾的。
所以我会说：我是在认真做，而这个制度让认真变得比它需要的难得多。如果规定每年用同样的措辞印在垃圾桶上，我猜绝大多数家庭不费任何力气就能做对。我不觉得现在这种难度对任何人有好处。
Hold my breath and count to thirty. It works maybe half the time, which I've come to think is roughly what any of these methods actually achieve.

The reason I'm sceptical about all of them is that nearly every remedy people swear by has the same structure underneath: it makes you concentrate on something else for about a minute. Sugar, holding your breath, drinking from the far side of a glass, being startled — the physical explanations offered for these are all different and mostly unconvincing, and the one thing they share is that you cannot do them absent-mindedly. Meanwhile hiccups usually stop on their own within a few minutes, so anything you do in that window gets the credit.

My grandmother swore by a spoonful of sugar and it genuinely did work on me as a child, every time. I've since become fairly sure that had less to do with the sugar than with a seven-year-old being given a spoonful of sugar, which is an event significant enough to command your entire attention. My brother's method is to drink water while bending forward, which looks absurd and works about as often as mine does. Nobody in my family will accept that these are the same method.

So my view is that the specific technique matters much less than whether it's distracting enough. If somebody told me a completely invented ritual with enough confidence, I'd expect it to work at about the same rate, and I'd probably keep using it.
屏住呼吸数到三十。大概有一半的时候管用，而我逐渐觉得，这差不多就是所有这类方法实际能达到的水平。
我对所有这些方法都有点怀疑，原因是几乎每一个大家信誓旦旦推荐的偏方，底下的结构都一样：它让你把注意力集中到别的东西上大约一分钟。吃糖、屏气、从杯子的另一侧喝水、被吓一跳——为这些提供的生理解释各不相同，而且大多不太有说服力，它们唯一的共同点是：你没法心不在焉地做这些事。与此同时，打嗝通常几分钟之内会自己停，所以在那个窗口里你做的任何事都会被记上功劳。
我奶奶一直坚信吃一勺糖最管用，而我小时候确实每次都有效。我后来相当确定，起作用的与其说是糖，不如说是“一个七岁小孩被给了一勺糖”这件事本身——那是一件重要到足以占据你全部注意力的事件。我弟弟的方法是弯着腰喝水，看起来非常荒唐，成功率和我的差不多。我们家没有一个人愿意承认这其实是同一种方法。
所以我的看法是：具体用什么方法远没有“它够不够分散注意力”重要。如果有人用足够自信的语气告诉我一个完全编出来的仪式，我估计它的成功率也差不多，而且我大概会一直用下去。
People who ask questions back. That's genuinely the whole filter — I'd take a curious person I disagree with over an agreeable person who doesn't ask me anything, every single time.

The reason is that a conversation where only one person is curious isn't a conversation, it's a performance with an audience of one, and I find it exhausting from either side. If I'm the one asking everything, I go home having learned things but feeling like I did a job. If I'm the one being asked everything, I go home slightly embarrassed at how much I talked. Neither of those is the thing I wanted when I agreed to meet somebody.

The friendship that has taught me most about this is with somebody I've known about ten years. Early on we fell into a habit of asking each other what we'd changed our minds about recently — it started as a joke, I think, or at least not seriously. But it turns out to be an almost unfailing question, because you can't answer it with a summary of your week. She once spent about forty minutes explaining why she'd reversed her position on something she'd argued the opposite of for years, and I've thought about that conversation more than most things I've read.

So I'd say shared interests matter much less to me than people assume. Two people who both like the same films can run out of things to say by nine o'clock. Two people who are both genuinely interested in what the other one thinks will not run out, and I've stopped optimising for anything else.
会反过来提问的人。这基本就是我全部的筛选标准——一个和我意见不同但有好奇心的人，和一个处处附和却什么都不问我的人，我每次都会选前者。
原因是，如果只有一个人好奇，那就不是对话，而是一场只有一名观众的表演，而无论站在哪一边我都觉得累。如果所有问题都是我在问，我回家时确实学到了东西，但感觉像干了一份活；如果所有问题都是别人在问我，我回家时会有点不好意思，因为我发现自己说了太多。这两种都不是我答应见面时想要的东西。
在这件事上教会我最多的，是一段十年左右的友谊。很早的时候我们养成了一个习惯，会互相问对方最近改变了什么想法——我记得一开始大概是当玩笑说的，至少不是很认真。但事实证明这个问题几乎从不失手，因为你没法用“这周过得怎么样”来敷衍它。有一次她花了大概四十分钟解释，她为什么在一件事上推翻了自己坚持多年的立场，而那次对话我想起的次数，比我读过的大部分东西都多。
所以我会说，共同爱好的重要性远比大家以为的低。两个都喜欢同一类电影的人，可能到九点就没话说了；而两个真心想知道对方在想什么的人不会没话说。我已经不再按别的标准去挑了。
History, comfortably — but I want to be honest that this had almost nothing to do with history. I've barely read any since, which rather gives the game away.

The reason is that we had a teacher who treated our opinions as things worth arguing with. That sounds like a small distinction and it isn't. Most teaching I encountered treated a fourteen-year-old's view as something to be gently corrected on the way to the right answer. He treated it as a position that had to be defended, which meant that having a view suddenly carried a cost, and that changed how carefully we formed them.

The lesson everybody in that class still remembers is one where he spent the entire hour letting us dismantle something he'd told us the week before. He'd given us an explanation for why a particular thing happened; over the weekend two students had found material that contradicted it; and rather than tidy that away he handed the hour over. By the end he said, in front of thirty of us, that he'd been overconfident about it. I was fifteen and I don't think I'd ever seen an adult do that. It was more instructive than the syllabus.

So what made it my favourite subject wasn't the content at all — it was the discovery that a subject could be argued with. I'd assumed until then that school subjects were lists of true things, and I've since noticed that the people who never had that lesson tend to treat their own opinions the same way.
历史课，而且是明显的第一名——不过我想老实说，这跟历史本身几乎没关系。从那以后我几乎没再读过历史书，这一点大概就露馅了。
原因是我们有一位老师，他把我们的看法当成值得认真反驳的东西。这听起来是个很小的区别，其实不是。我遇到的大多数教学，会把一个十四岁孩子的观点当成一个需要被温和纠正、然后走向标准答案的东西。而他把它当成一个必须被辩护的立场，这意味着“有一个看法”突然是有代价的，于是我们形成看法时就认真多了。
那个班上所有人到现在还记得的一节课，是他用整整一节课让我们拆解他上一周告诉我们的东西。他给过我们一个解释，说明某件事为什么发生；周末有两个同学找到了和这个解释矛盾的材料。他没有把这件事轻轻带过，而是把那节课交了出来。到最后，他当着我们三十个人的面说，他当初对那个说法过于自信了。我那年十五岁，我想我此前没见过一个大人这样做。那比课程大纲有用得多。
所以让它成为我最喜欢的课的，完全不是内容，而是我发现了一件事：一门学科是可以被反驳的。在那之前我一直以为学校里的科目就是一串正确的事实。后来我注意到，那些从没上过这一课的人，往往也是这样对待自己的观点的。
A friend I met when we were both fourteen, so it's coming up on twenty years. We've lived in the same city for maybe four of those, which I think is part of why it has lasted.

What I value most about her is completely unglamorous: she tells me when she thinks I'm wrong. That is much rarer than people admit. Most friendships settle into a comfortable arrangement where the unspoken deal is that we each support whatever the other has already decided, and that's pleasant, and it's also useless at exactly the moments you need a friend most. She has never signed up to that deal, and there have been years where I found her genuinely annoying because of it.

The clearest instance was about six years ago, when I was three weeks from accepting a job I was obviously unhappy about. Everyone else congratulated me. She asked me one question — she asked what I'd say if she took it instead — and I heard myself list four reasons she shouldn't. I turned it down eight days later. That job's team, as it happens, was restructured out of existence within the year, so she was accidentally right twice, but that's not really the point. The point is that eleven people had the information and one of them said it out loud.

So if you asked me the secret of a friendship lasting twenty years, I'd say it's that it was never only comfortable. Comfort is what makes a friendship pleasant. Being willing to be briefly unwelcome is what makes it durable.
一个我十四岁认识的朋友，到现在快二十年了。这二十年里我们大概只有四年住在同一个城市，我觉得这反而是它能维持下来的原因之一。
我最看重她的一点一点都不浪漫：她认为我错的时候会直接说。这比大家承认的要稀有得多。大多数友谊最后会稳定成一种舒服的安排，默认的交易是：不管对方已经决定了什么，我们都支持。这很愉快，但恰恰在你最需要朋友的时刻毫无用处。她从来没有加入过这个交易，也确实有那么几年，我因此觉得她挺烦的。
最清楚的一次是大概六年前，我离接受一份自己明显不开心的工作只剩三个星期。所有人都在恭喜我。她只问了我一个问题——她问，如果换成她去接这份工作，我会怎么说——然后我听见自己一口气列了四条她不该去的理由。八天后我拒绝了那份工作。碰巧的是，那个团队在一年之内就被重组掉了，所以她无意中对了两次，不过这不是重点。重点是当时有十一个人掌握着同样的信息，而只有一个人把它说了出来。
所以你要问我一段友谊维持二十年的秘诀，我会说：因为它从来不只是舒服的。舒服让一段友谊愉快，而愿意短暂地不受欢迎，才让它耐用。
An online encyclopaedia, which I'm aware is a boring answer. I did try to think of something more interesting and everything else I came up with I use rather than enjoy.

The reason it wins is the ratio of questions in to questions out. It's the only site I open with one question and leave an hour later holding six, and every other site I use is designed to do the opposite — to answer the thing and then hold onto you. There's also the fact that nothing on it is trying to be timely. Everything I read there could have been read a year ago or a year from now, which turns out to be restful in a way I didn't appreciate until I noticed how much of the rest of my reading has a shelf life of about nine hours.

The most recent illustration was last week. I opened it to check a single date for something I was writing — I needed the year a particular treaty was signed, which took about eight seconds. Forty minutes later I was reading about the history of the tea trade, having got there through four or five links I couldn't now reconstruct, and I had entirely stopped caring about the date. I did eventually go back and use it. The forty minutes produced nothing except that I now know roughly why tea is grown where it's grown.

So the reason I'd name it as a favourite is precisely that it wastes my time well. Most things that take an hour from me leave me feeling that I've been had. That one doesn't, and I think the difference is that I chose every step of the path.
一个在线百科网站，我知道这是个无聊的答案。我确实努力想过更有意思的选项，但我想到的其他网站都是我在“使用”，而不是在“享受”。
它之所以胜出，是因为“带进去的问题”和“带出来的问题”的比例。它是唯一一个我带着一个问题打开、一个小时后带着六个问题离开的网站，而我用的其他网站都是为了相反的目的设计的——先回答你那个问题，然后把你留住。还有一点是，它上面的东西都不追求时效。我在那儿读到的任何内容，一年前读或者一年后读都一样，而这一点带来的松弛感，是我直到注意到自己其他阅读的保质期大概只有九个小时之后，才体会到的。
最近的一个例子是上个星期。我打开它只是为了查一个日期，我写东西要用到某个条约签订的年份，那花了大概八秒。四十分钟以后，我在读茶叶贸易史，中间经过了四五个我现在已经还原不出来的链接，而我早就不关心那个日期了。我最后当然还是回去用了它。那四十分钟什么都没产生，除了我现在大致知道了茶为什么种在它现在种的那些地方。
所以我会把它列为最喜欢的网站，理由恰恰是它把我的时间浪费得很好。大部分拿走我一个小时的东西，都会让我觉得自己被算计了；它不会。我想区别在于，那条路上的每一步都是我自己选的。

open: What I would say is that the interesting question is not how much, it is what it is standing in for — and that reframing is the only thing on this subject that ever changed my behaviour.
我会说：真正有意思的问题不是“多少”，而是它在替代什么——而在这个话题上，唯一真正改变过我行为的，就是这个重新表述。

The reason is that quantity is downstream of function. If something is doing a job for you — winding down, filling a silence, making a room easier to be in — then reducing the quantity without replacing the job just makes you worse at the thing it was handling. Every attempt I made to change this by counting failed within a month, and the one that worked started with working out what the counting was actually about.
原因是，数量是功能的下游。如果某样东西在替你做一份工作——收尾放松、填补沉默、让一个房间更容易待——那么在没有替代那份工作的情况下减少数量，只会让你在它原本处理的那件事上更笨拙。我所有靠“计数”来改变这件事的尝试，都在一个月内失败了；而唯一奏效的那次，是从弄清楚那个计数究竟是关于什么开始的。

The specific case is that mine was almost entirely a signal that the working day was over. Nothing to do with taste and not much to do with the effect — it was a full stop. Once I saw that, the fix was not restraint, it was finding another full stop. I settled on a twenty-minute walk at the same time, which sounds feeble as a substitute and worked immediately, because it was doing the same job.
具体到我身上：它几乎完全是一个“工作日结束了”的信号。和味道没什么关系，和效果也关系不大——它是一个句号。看清这一点之后，解决办法不是克制，而是找到另一个句号。我最后定的是在同一时间走二十分钟。作为替代品这听起来很无力，但它立刻就奏效了，因为它在做同一份工作。

So my answer is that I would ask anybody, including myself, what the habit is for before asking how much of it there is. The second question is unanswerable in a useful way until you have done the first.
所以我的答案是：我会先问任何人——包括我自己——这个习惯是为了什么，然后才问它有多少。在你做完第一个问题之前，第二个问题是没法有用地回答的。
opinion: My position is that the framing most of these debates use is the problem, and that I would rather argue about the framing than about where the line goes.
我的立场是：这类辩论惯用的那个框架本身才是问题；比起争论那条线画在哪里，我更愿意争论这个框架。

The reason is that almost every public argument here is conducted as though the choice were between permission and prohibition, when in practice what determines outcomes is neither. It is what happens around the thing — whether somebody in difficulty can say so without consequence, whether help is easy to reach, whether the honest conversation is available. Those are not the parts anybody argues about, and they are the parts that move the numbers.
原因是，这里几乎所有公共争论进行的方式，都好像选择只在“允许”和“禁止”之间；而实际上决定结果的两者都不是。真正起作用的是围绕这件事发生的一切——一个陷入困难的人能不能说出来而不必承担后果，帮助好不好找，那场诚实的对话在不在。这些都不是有人在争论的部分，而它们才是让数字发生变化的部分。

What convinced me was watching two situations with essentially the same facts go completely differently. Same substance, same quantity, comparable people. In one case the person in trouble was surrounded by an arrangement where saying so was normal and it was dealt with early. In the other it was unsayable for about two years, and by the time it was said the problem was much larger. The formal rules were identical in both. Everything that mattered was in the informal part.
让我确信这一点的，是我看着两件事实基本相同的事，走向了完全不同的结局。同样的东西，同样的量，处境相仿的人。其中一个陷入麻烦的人，身边的环境让“说出来”是正常的，于是它很早就被处理了；另一个则有大概两年说不出口，而等到说出来的时候，问题已经大得多了。两边的正式规则一模一样，所有起作用的东西都在非正式的那一部分里。

So my answer is that I hold a view on the usual question and I do not think the usual question is where the leverage is. If I could change one thing it would be how easy it is to admit to it, which is not a policy anybody campaigns on.
所以我的答案是：我对那个惯常的问题有看法，但我不认为杠杆在那里。如果我只能改一件事，我会改“承认它有多容易”——而这不是任何人会拿去竞选的政策。

open: The honest answer is something small from this week rather than anything I would have prepared, and I have come to think that is the correct way to answer this kind of question.
诚实的回答是这周发生的某件小事，而不是任何我事先准备好的东西；而我逐渐认为，这才是回答这类问题的正确方式。

The reason is that small talk gets a bad name because people try to make it impressive, and an impressive answer to a light question kills the exchange — the other person now has to match it, and they cannot, so they say something polite and the conversation ends. A small, specific, slightly odd detail does the opposite. It is easy to respond to, it does not require the other person to compete, and it gives them somewhere to go.
原因是，闲聊之所以名声不好，是因为人们总想把它说得体面；而对一个轻松的问题给出体面的答案，会把交流杀死——对方现在得拿出同等级别的东西来接，可他接不上，于是说一句客气话，谈话就结束了。一个小的、具体的、略微古怪的细节效果正好相反：它容易回应，不要求对方跟你比，而且给了他一个可以往下走的地方。

The test I use is whether my answer contains something the other person could ask a follow-up about. If I say the week has been fine, there is nothing to grab. If I say I spent forty minutes on Tuesday trying to work out where a draught in my flat was coming from and never found it, that is not more interesting in itself, but it has handles on it. In my experience the second kind of answer gets a real reply about eight times out of ten and the first gets one about twice.
我用的检验标准是：我的答案里有没有对方可以追问的东西。如果我说这周还行，那就什么都抓不住；如果我说周二我花了四十分钟找我家那股穿堂风是从哪儿来的、最后也没找到，这件事本身并不更有意思，但它上面有把手。按我的经验，第二种答案十次里大概有八次能换来真正的回应，第一种大概只有两次。
So I aim low and specific rather than high and general. Small talk is not a test of how interesting you are, it is a test of whether you left the other person anything to say.
所以我瞄得低而具体，不瞄高而笼统。闲聊不是在考你有多有趣，是在考你有没有给对方留下可说的东西。
What I would say now is about how somebody behaves when something goes wrong, which is not where I would have looked ten years ago.
我现在会说的是：一个人在出问题的时候怎么表现。而十年前我看的完全不是这个地方。

The reason is that everything visible early on is a performance in the honest sense — not dishonest, just the version of a person that is available when nothing is being tested. You learn very little from how somebody is on a good evening, because almost everybody is fine on a good evening. What tells you something is a cancelled plan, a mistake, a piece of bad news that arrives while you are together, because those are the moments where the actual operating rules show.
原因是，早期能看见的一切都是一种表演——不是虚伪那个意思，只是一个人在什么都没被检验时能拿出来的那个版本。从一个愉快的晚上能学到的东西非常少，因为几乎所有人在愉快的晚上都不错。真正能说明问题的，是一个被取消的约、一个错误、一条在你们在一起时到达的坏消息，因为那些时刻才会露出真正在运行的规则。

The clearest thing I have seen, and it changed how I look at this entirely, was watching somebody deal with being wrong about something small in front of other people. It was a trivial matter — a fact, an argument about nothing. They said they had been wrong, said it early, and then moved on without needing to be reassured about it. It took ten seconds. I remember thinking that I had just learned more in those ten seconds than in the previous two months of extremely pleasant conversation.
我见过最清楚的一次，也彻底改变了我看这件事的方式：我看着一个人在别人面前，处理自己在一件小事上弄错了。那件事微不足道——一个事实，一场关于什么都不是的争论。那个人说自己错了，很早就说了，然后就翻篇了，不需要别人反过来安慰。整个过程十秒钟。我记得当时心里想：这十秒钟里我学到的，比之前两个月极其愉快的谈话都多。

So the thing I pay attention to now is friction rather than chemistry. Chemistry tells you the first three months will be enjoyable. How somebody is when it is not going well tells you about everything after that.
所以我现在注意的是摩擦，而不是来电。来电告诉你的是前三个月会很愉快；一个人在事情不顺利时是什么样，告诉你的是那之后的一切。
yesno: Yes, and I would give the same answer now that I would have given at twenty-two, which is not true of many things.
是的，而且我现在给的答案，和我二十二岁时会给的一样——这在很多事上都不成立。

The reason it has not moved is that it turns out to rest on something quite basic about how I am rather than on any theory I hold about relationships. I have revised most of my views in this area — about timing, about how much difference you can absorb, about what is worth arguing over — but this particular one has survived every revision, which is usually a sign that it is not really an opinion at all.
它之所以没有变过，是因为它最后落脚的地方，是关于我这个人比较根本的某样东西，而不是我持有的任何一套关于亲密关系的理论。这个领域里我大部分看法都修改过——关于时机，关于能吸收多大的差异，关于什么值得吵——唯独这一条挺过了每一次修改，而这通常说明它其实根本不是一个观点。

The closest I came to changing it was a stretch of about a year where I was in a situation that ran on the opposite principle, and I made a genuine effort to adapt rather than to object. I was not pretending; I wanted it to work and I gave it a real attempt. What I found was that I could manage it for a few months and then could not, and that the cost showed up somewhere I was not expecting — not in arguments but in how much I was talking, which dropped off almost completely without my noticing.
我离改变它最近的一次，是大概一年时间里，我处在一个按相反原则运行的关系中，而我是真心想去适应，而不是去反对的。我不是在装；我希望它成立，也确实认真试过。我发现的是：我能撑几个月，然后就撑不住了；而且代价出现在我没预料到的地方——不是在争吵上，而是在我说话的量上，它几乎完全掉下去了，而我自己都没察觉。
So it is a yes I have actually tested rather than assumed, which is the only reason I am willing to state it flatly. Everything else I believe about this subject I would put much more carefully.
所以这是一个我真的验证过、而不是想当然的“是”。也正因为如此，我才愿意把它说得这么干脆。关于这个话题我相信的其他一切，我都会说得谨慎得多。
Yes, and I will answer it directly, because I have found that hedging on this subject helps nobody — least of all the person who asked.
是的。而我会直接回答，因为我发现在这个话题上打太极对谁都没有好处——尤其是对提问的那个人。

The reason is that questions in this area are usually asked by somebody who has a reason to ask, and a careful non-answer leaves them alone with it. I have been on both sides of that. What I wanted when I was the one asking was not comfort and certainly not advice; it was evidence that the thing I was going through was something other people had also been through and come out of. A direct answer provides that. A cautious one provides nothing.
原因是，这个领域的问题通常是有理由才会被问出来的；而一个小心翼翼的“不回答”，等于把对方一个人留在原地。这两边我都待过。当我是提问的那一方时，我想要的不是安慰，更绝对不是建议；我想要的是一个证据：我正在经历的事，别人也经历过，而且走出来了。一个直接的回答能提供这个，一个谨慎的回答什么都提供不了。

What taught me this was somebody answering me plainly at a point when everybody around me was being extremely careful. They said what had happened to them, in ordinary language, without softening it and without turning it into a lesson. It took about two minutes and it was the single most useful thing anybody said to me that year — not because the content was remarkable, but because it established that this was a survivable category of experience rather than a private catastrophe.
教会我这一点的，是在我周围所有人都极其小心的时候，有一个人直白地回答了我。他用平常的语言说了发生在他身上的事，没有软化，也没有把它变成一堂课。整个过程大概两分钟，而那是那一年里任何人对我说过的最有用的一句话——不是因为内容有多特别，而是因为它确立了一件事：这是一类人能活着走过去的经历，而不是一场私人的灾难。
So the answer is yes, and I would say the same to somebody I had just met, because that is exactly the situation in which a plain answer does the most work.
所以答案是肯定的。而且我对刚认识的人也会这么说，因为那恰恰是一个直白的回答最能起作用的情境。

open: What I go back to is almost always about ordinary people doing ordinary things, and I went through a long period of being slightly embarrassed by that before I worked out why it was the case.
我会反复回去的，几乎总是那些写普通人做普通事的东西。有很长一段时间我为此有点不好意思，直到我弄明白了原因。

The reason is that a big plot leaves me nothing to hold afterwards. I follow it, I reach the end, and a month later it is gone. Whereas a character who reminds me of somebody I actually know stays, because every time I see that person I get the story back. It is a slightly parasitic way to read or watch — I am using the thing to think about my own life — but I have stopped pretending otherwise, and once I admitted it my taste made a lot more sense to me.
原因是，宏大的情节在结束之后不给我留下任何可以抓住的东西。我跟着读，读到结尾，一个月后就没了。而一个让我想起身边某个真实的人的角色会留下来，因为每次我见到那个人，那个故事就回来了。这种读法或看法确实有点“寄生”——我是在借它想我自己的生活——但我已经不装作不是这样了；而一旦承认，我的品味对我自己就说得通多了。

The clearest evidence is a novel I have now read three times, about five years apart. At twenty I was certain it was about the daughter, because I was the daughter's age. At thirty it was obviously about the mother, and I was slightly shocked to find I had missed her completely the first time. Last year the person I could not stop watching was an uncle I had previously registered as more or less furniture. Same book, three different books. Plot cannot do that.
最清楚的证据是一本小说，我到现在读了三遍，大概每隔五年一次。二十岁时我确信它写的是女儿，因为我和女儿差不多大。三十岁再读，它明显写的是母亲，而我很吃惊自己第一次完全没看见她。去年我一直盯着看的人，变成了一个我此前印象里差不多等于家具的舅舅。同一本书，三本不同的书。情节做不到这一点。

So what I look for is recognition rather than surprise. Surprise is enjoyable once. Recognition is something you can return to as you turn into different people, and that is a much better return on three hundred pages.
所以我找的是熟悉感，而不是意外。意外好看一次；熟悉感是你可以在自己变成不同的人之后再回去的东西，而这三百页的回报要高得多。
yesno: Yes, and considerably more than I admit when the subject comes up in a group, which is itself part of the answer.
是的，而且比我在一群人面前提到这个话题时承认的多得多——而这一点本身就是答案的一部分。

The reason I understate it is that this is one of the areas where people quietly rank each other, and the ranking has almost nothing to do with enjoyment. There is a version of taste that exists to be reported rather than experienced, and I spent a fair stretch of my twenties assembling one. What I actually returned to in private and what I would have listed in company were two different sets, and the private one was the honest account.
我之所以说得保守，是因为这是人们会悄悄互相排名的领域之一，而那个排名和享受几乎没有关系。存在一种“为了被报告而不是被体验”的品味，我二十多岁有相当一段时间都在拼装这样一套。我私下真正会重看重听的，和我在人前会列出来的，是两份不同的名单，而私下那份才是诚实的说法。

What broke it was noticing, around thirty, that I had stopped finishing things I did not enjoy. Not as a principle — I just started putting them down. Within about a year the gap between the two lists had closed, mostly by the reported list getting less impressive. I now abandon something about a third of the way in without any guilt at all, and the result is that I get through more and remember more of it, which is the opposite of what I expected.
打破它的，是我三十岁前后注意到：我已经不再把不喜欢的东西看完了。这不是什么原则——我只是开始把它们放下。大概一年之内，那两份名单之间的差距就消失了，主要是因为“被报告的那份”变得没那么体面了。我现在会在大概三分之一处放弃一样东西，一点内疚都没有；结果是我看完的更多，记住的也更多，这和我预期的正好相反。

So it is a yes, and the more useful part of the answer is that I stopped treating this as a subject with a right answer. Once it is only about what you actually return to, the question gets a lot easier.
所以答案是肯定的。而这个回答里更有用的部分是：我不再把这件事当成一个有标准答案的题目。一旦它只关于你真正会回去的东西，这个问题就容易多了。
Yes, and it is one of the few habits I have that survived contact with a busy year, which is the only test I trust any more.
是的，而且这是我为数不多、挺过了一整个忙碌年份的习惯，而那是我现在唯一相信的检验。

The reason it survived is that it costs almost nothing to do and it is attached to something I would be doing anyway. Every habit I have tried to install as a separate item on a list has died within about six weeks — the gym at seven, the language app, the journal. The ones that lasted are all bolted onto something already fixed in the day, so there is no decision involved and nothing to remember.
它之所以能活下来，是因为做起来几乎没有成本，而且挂在一件我本来就要做的事上。我试过的每一个作为清单上独立项目安装的习惯，都在大约六周内死掉了——七点去健身房、语言应用、写日记。留下来的那些，全都是嫁接在一天里已经固定的某件事上，所以不涉及任何决定，也不需要记住。

The concrete version is that I do it while the kettle boils, which is between two and three minutes, twice a day, whether or not I feel like it. That framing is the whole trick. If I had set out to do six minutes a day deliberately I would have failed inside a month, because six minutes deliberately is a thing you can put off; two minutes while you are standing there anyway is not. I have kept it up for about two years now and I have missed maybe a fortnight in total, mostly while travelling.
具体的版本是：我在烧水的时候做，也就是两三分钟，一天两次，不管想不想做。这个安排本身就是全部的诀窍。如果我当初立志每天专门做六分钟，一个月内一定失败，因为“专门做六分钟”是一件可以往后拖的事；而“反正你就站在那儿的两分钟”不是。到现在我坚持了大概两年，一共大概只断过两个星期，主要是在出门在外的时候。
So my answer is yes, and what I would actually pass on is not the habit but the method: attach it to something that already happens, keep it under three minutes, and never make it a decision.
所以我的回答是肯定的。而我真正想传下去的不是这个习惯本身，而是那个方法：把它挂在已经会发生的事情上，控制在三分钟以内，并且永远不要让它变成一个决定。
open: The part of my day I would actually defend is a small window in the morning that has no purpose attached to it, and I would give up a great deal before I gave that up.
我一天里真正会守住的，是早上那一小段没有任何目的的时间。要我放弃它之前，我可以先放弃很多别的东西。

The reason it matters is that everything else in a day is spoken for. Work has a claim on it, other people have a claim on it, and even the things I do for pleasure tend to arrive with an expectation — read this, learn that, get better at something. An hour with nothing wanting anything from it turns out to be the thing that makes the rest of the day survivable, and I did not understand that until I lost it for a while and noticed the difference.
它之所以重要，是因为一天里其他所有时间都已经被认领了。工作对它有主张，别人对它有主张，甚至我为了乐趣做的事，也往往带着某种期待——读完这个、学会那个、在某方面变得更好。而一段“没有任何东西对它有要求”的时间，最后成了让这一天其余部分可以撑下来的东西。我是在有一阵子失去它、并注意到差别之后，才明白这一点的。

In practice it is about forty minutes, before anybody else is up, and the rule is that I do not look at a screen during it. I make something to drink, I sit in the same chair, and quite often I do nothing identifiable at all. The one time I tried to make it productive — I decided I would use it to study — it stopped working within two weeks, and I have not made that mistake again. The moment it acquired a purpose it stopped doing the thing I needed it for.
实际操作上大概是四十分钟，在别人起床之前，规矩是这段时间不看屏幕。我泡点东西喝，坐在同一张椅子上，而且相当多的时候什么可指认的事都没做。我唯一一次试图让它变得“有产出”——我决定用它来学习——两个星期之内它就失效了，而这个错我没再犯第二次。它一旦获得了目的，就不再提供我需要的那个东西了。
So if you asked me to describe my everyday life, I would describe it around that window rather than around the work, because the work changes every couple of years and that has not changed in eight.
所以如果你让我描述我的日常生活，我会围绕那一段时间来描述，而不是围绕工作。因为工作每隔几年就会变，而它八年没有变过。

It comes back to my mother, though not for the reason people usually expect when they ask about family. It is not a sentimental thing — it is that she is the person whose habits I can see in myself most clearly now that I am old enough to notice.
最后总会回到我妈身上，不过原因跟大家问家庭时预期的不太一样。这不是什么感情用事，而是我现在年纪够大了，能在自己身上最清楚地看见她的那些习惯。

The reason I keep landing there is that you do not choose what you absorb at home. You absorb it before you know that absorbing is happening, and by the time you are old enough to have opinions about it, it is already how you do things. I spent most of my twenties assuming I had built myself from scratch, and most of my thirties finding out how much of me arrived pre-installed.
我之所以总是落到这一点上，是因为你在家里吸收的东西不是你选的。它在你还不知道“吸收”这回事的时候就发生了，等你大到能对它有看法，它已经变成你做事的方式了。我二十多岁的时候一直以为自己是白手起家造出来的，三十多岁才发现，我身上有多少东西是出厂就装好的。

The clearest instance is small and slightly embarrassing. My mother has always dealt with a difficult conversation by cleaning something first — she will wash up an already clean pan for ten minutes and then say the thing she came in to say. I noticed about two years ago that I do exactly this. Not consciously, and not because I learned it as a technique; I just found myself wiping down a worktop before telling a friend something awkward, and heard her voice in my own hands. I have stopped fighting it. It works.
最清楚的例子很小，而且有点难为情。我妈处理一场难开口的谈话，永远是先去擦点什么——她会把一口本来就干净的锅洗上十分钟，然后才说她进来要说的那句话。大概两年前我发现，我做的一模一样。不是有意识的，也不是我把它当技巧学来的；我只是在告诉一个朋友一件尴尬的事之前，发现自己在擦台面，然后从自己的手上听见了她的声音。我已经不跟这件事较劲了，因为它确实有用。

So when a question is about family I do not really answer with facts about them. I answer with what I can see of them in me, because that is the part that is still active, and it is a far more honest account than a list of where everybody was born.
所以碰到关于家庭的问题，我不太会用事实去回答。我回答的是我能在自己身上看见的他们，因为那才是还在起作用的那部分，而且比一串“谁在哪里出生”的清单诚实得多。
yesno: Yes, and it took me a long time to be able to say that without adding a defensive sentence after it.
是的，而且我花了很久，才能说完这句话不再补一句自我辩护。

The reason it was hard is that families are the one subject where you are expected to have a settled position, and most people's is genuinely mixed. If you say yes you sound as though you are claiming everything was fine, and if you say no you sound as though you are filing a complaint. The truth for most of us is that both things are true about the same house at the same time, and that a straight answer either way is a simplification you make for the sake of the person asking.
难说出口的原因是，家庭是唯一一件大家默认你必须有明确立场的事，而大多数人的立场其实是混合的。你说“是”，听起来像在声称一切都很好；你说“不是”，听起来像在提出控诉。而对我们大多数人来说，真相是：同一个家里，同一段时间，这两件事同时成立；无论选哪一边，直接给一个答案都是为了照顾提问的人而做的简化。

What changed it for me was a conversation with my brother about four years ago, in which we compared notes on something we had both been present for as children and discovered we remembered it completely differently. Not slightly — differently enough that one of us had to be substantially wrong. Neither of us was lying. We were four years apart and had been standing in different parts of the same room, and that was enough. Since then I have held my own version much more loosely.
改变我想法的是大概四年前和我弟弟的一次谈话。我们对照了一件我们小时候都在场的事，结果发现记忆完全不同。不是稍有出入，而是不同到我们其中一个必然记错得相当离谱。我们谁都没有说谎。我们差四岁，当时站在同一个房间的不同位置，这就够了。从那以后，我对自己那个版本抓得松多了。
So the answer is yes, with the understanding that it is my yes and my brother would give you a different one, and that both accounts are honest. I have stopped needing mine to be the correct one.
所以答案是肯定的，但要理解：这是我的“是”，我弟弟会给你另一个，而两份说法都是诚实的。我已经不再需要我这份是正确的那份了。

open: What I have learned to do is change where I am rather than try to change how I feel, and that took an embarrassingly long time to arrive at.
我学会的做法是改变自己所在的位置，而不是试图改变自己的感受；而我花了很不好意思承认的时间才走到这一步。

The reason is that a mood indoors has nothing to push against. You sit with it, it fills the available space, and after two hours it has stopped being about whatever started it and has become a general position about your life. I spent years trying to think my way out of that, which is a bit like trying to argue with the weather. What actually interrupts it is movement, and I do not think it is really about exercise — it is that the scenery changes every few seconds, and a mood needs a stable environment to grow in.
原因是，一种情绪待在屋里，没有任何东西可以顶着它。你陪着它坐，它就把可用的空间全填满；两个小时以后，它已经不是关于最初那件事了，而变成了关于你整个人生的一个结论。我有好些年一直想靠思考走出去，那有点像跟天气讲道理。真正能打断它的是移动，而我觉得这跟运动其实关系不大——是外面的景象每几秒就变一次，而一种情绪需要一个稳定的环境才能长大。

The clearest test was last winter, during a fairly grim few weeks. I made myself walk for twenty minutes every evening — not far, not scenic, the same three streets in the dark. The first three days I resented every minute. By the Wednesday of the second week I noticed I was going out slightly earlier than I had to, and by the Friday I felt noticeably better, with nothing in my circumstances having changed at all.
最清楚的一次验证是去年冬天，那几周过得相当糟。我逼自己每天晚上走二十分钟——不远，也没什么风景，就是在黑暗里绕同样的三条街。头三天我每一分钟都不情愿。到第二周的星期三，我发现自己出门的时间比必须出门的时间稍微早了一点；到星期五我明显感觉好多了，而我的处境一点都没变。
So my honest answer is that I do not try to cheer myself up, because I have never once managed it by deciding to. I move, and the feeling usually follows within about a quarter of an hour.
所以我诚实的回答是：我不试图让自己开心起来，因为我从来没有靠“决定开心”成功过一次。我动起来，然后感受通常会在一刻钟之内跟上。
yesno: Yes, and I am aware that answering that quickly is itself part of what the question is asking about.
是的。而我也知道，回答得这么快，本身就是这个问题想问的一部分。

The reason I can answer quickly is that I have been asked some version of it enough times to have thought about it properly, which was not true five years ago. Back then I would have given whichever answer sounded better and believed it while I was saying it. What changed is not that I became more honest — it is that I got enough evidence about my own behaviour that the flattering answer stopped being available to me.
我之所以能快速回答，是因为这个问题的各种版本我被问过够多次，多到已经认真想过；而五年前并不是这样。那时候我会给出听起来更好的那个答案，而且在说的当下自己也相信。改变的不是我变得更诚实了——而是我积累了足够多关于自己行为的证据，多到那个好听的答案对我来说已经不可用了。

The evidence, in this case, was noticing a pattern across about a year. The same situation kept arising, roughly every couple of months, and I kept responding to it in the same way while telling myself each time that this instance was different. It was not different. Somewhere around the fourth or fifth repetition I had to accept that I was looking at a standing tendency rather than a series of coincidences, and once you have counted it you cannot go back to describing it as unusual.
就这件事而言，证据是我注意到了一个跨越大约一年的模式。同一种情况反复出现，大概每两个月一次，而我每次都用同样的方式回应，同时每次都告诉自己“这一回不一样”。它并没有不一样。大概到第四次或第五次重复的时候，我不得不承认：我看到的是一个长期存在的倾向，而不是一串巧合。而一旦你数过了，你就没法再把它描述成偶然了。
So the answer is yes, and I would add that I only know it because I stopped taking each occasion on its own terms and started noticing how often it happened.
所以答案是肯定的。我还要补一句：我之所以知道，是因为我不再就事论事地看每一次，而开始注意它发生的频率。

open: The thing I would name is not a dish, it is a habit — that I cook the same handful of things over and over rather than trying something new, and I have come round to thinking that is the point rather than a failure of ambition.
我会说的不是某道菜，而是一个习惯：我会把同样的那几样反复做，而不是不断尝试新的。我后来逐渐认为，这恰恰是重点，而不是缺乏进取心。

The reason is that repetition is what turns cooking from a project into something you can do on a Tuesday when you are tired. A dish you have made forty times takes no decisions: you do not measure, you do not read anything, and you can hold a conversation while you do it. A new recipe takes the whole evening and your full attention, and there are only so many evenings where that is what I want.
原因是，重复才能把做饭从一个“项目”变成一件你在星期二很累的时候也能做的事。一道你做过四十次的菜不需要任何决定：你不用量，不用看任何东西，而且可以一边做一边聊天。一个新菜谱要占掉整个晚上和你全部的注意力，而我想要那样的晚上，总共就那么几个。

The concrete case is a soup my grandmother used to make. I asked her about it twice and got a version with no measurements in it — a handful of this, cook it until it looks right. Last year I finally got there by making it badly four times in a row and adjusting each time. The fourth one tasted like hers. I have made it eleven or twelve times since, and I no longer think about it at all while I am doing it, which is exactly what I wanted.
具体的例子是我奶奶以前常做的一道汤。我问过她两次，得到的说法里都没有分量——这个抓一把，煮到看起来差不多就行。去年我终于做出来了，方法是连着做砸四次，每次调一点。第四次的味道和她做的一样。从那以后我又做了十一二次，而且现在做的时候脑子里完全不想它了——这正是我想要的。
So my answer is that I would rather have six things I can make without thinking than sixty I have made once. It is a less interesting answer at a dinner party and it is what actually gets eaten.
所以我的回答是：比起做过一次的六十样，我宁愿有六样是我不用想就能做出来的。这个答案在饭局上没那么有意思，但它才是真正被吃掉的那个。
yesno: Yes, though it is an acquired position rather than a natural one, and the acquiring took a few years and a certain amount of discomfort.
是的，不过这是练出来的，不是天生的，而且这个练的过程花了几年，也伴随着一定程度的不适。

The reason it changed is that I stopped treating my preferences in this area as facts about me and started treating them as a current setting. For a long time I would say I did not like something as though reporting a fixed property, when what I actually meant was that I had tried it twice, badly prepared, some years ago. Almost everything I now genuinely enjoy is on a list I would once have ruled out, and the pattern is consistent enough that I no longer trust a first reaction.
它之所以改变，是因为我不再把这方面的偏好当成关于我的事实，而开始把它当成一个当前的设定。有很长一段时间，我说自己不喜欢某样东西时，语气像是在报告一个固定属性；而我实际的意思只是：我在若干年前试过两次，而且做得不好。我现在真心喜欢的东西，几乎全都在一份我当年会直接排除的名单上，而这个规律一致到我已经不再相信第一反应了。

The clearest instance was the first time I ate properly spiced food, at about twenty-four. Somebody ordered for the table and I could not finish my portion — I got two-thirds through and had to stop, sweating, while everybody else carried on talking. What struck me was that they were not enduring it, they were enjoying it, and I could tell the difference. I went back to the same place four or five times over the following year, deliberately building up. There is now a jar of chilli oil that lives permanently on my table.
最清楚的一次是我大概二十四岁时第一次吃到真正够味的菜。有人替全桌点了菜，我是真的吃不完自己那份——吃了三分之二就得停下来，一头汗，而其他人还在照常聊天。让我震动的是，他们不是在忍，是在享受，而这两者我分得出来。之后一年里我特意又去了那家店四五次，一点点往上加。现在我家餐桌上常年放着一罐辣椒油。
So it is a yes, and what I would pass on is that most people who think they do not like something are about eight attempts away from liking it.
所以答案是肯定的。而我想传下去的是：大多数以为自己不喜欢某样东西的人，其实只差大约八次尝试。

hypo: My honest answer is duller than the question invites, and I have decided that is the more interesting way to play it.
我诚实的回答，比这个问题所邀请的要平淡；而我认定，这样玩反而更有意思。

The reason is that hypotheticals like this have an obvious fun answer that everybody reaches for, and reaching for it tells the other person nothing they did not already know. The version worth giving is the one where you take the premise literally and think about what you would actually do on the Tuesday afterwards, once the novelty had gone. That is where these questions stop being a party game and start being about the person answering.
原因是，这类假设题都有一个显而易见的、好玩的答案，所有人都会伸手去拿；而拿了它，对面的人并不会知道任何他原本不知道的事。真正值得给出的版本，是你把前提当真，然后去想：新鲜劲儿过去之后，接下来那个星期二你实际上会做什么。那才是这类问题不再是聚会游戏、而开始关于回答的人的地方。

I know this because a few years ago somebody asked me one of these and I gave the impressive answer, and they pushed — they asked what I would do in the second month. I had nothing. I had never thought past the opening scene, because the opening scene is all these questions usually require. Working it out on the spot, out loud, I ended up describing something much smaller and much closer to my current life than I expected, and it was easily the most revealing thing I said that evening.
我知道这一点，是因为几年前有人问了我一个这样的问题，我给了那个体面的答案，而对方追问了——他问我第二个月会做什么。我答不上来。我从来没想过开场之后的事，因为开场就是这类问题通常需要的全部。当场出声地想下去，我最后描述出来的东西，比我预期的小得多，也离我现在的生活近得多；而那毫无疑问是我那天晚上说过的最能说明问题的一句话。

So I would take the premise seriously rather than enjoy it, and I would answer for the second month rather than the first. It is a slower answer and it is the one that actually gets a conversation going.
所以我会认真对待这个前提，而不是享受它；而且我会回答第二个月，而不是第一个月。这个答案更慢，但它才是真正能把对话打开的那一个。
choice: I would take the first one, and I want to say straight away that it is close — because pretending otherwise is where these questions usually go wrong.
我会选第一个，而且我想马上说明：两个差得不多——因为假装不是这样，正是这类问题通常出错的地方。

The reason it is close is that questions of this shape are constructed so that both sides have something real going for them; if one option were obviously better it would not be worth asking. So the useful part of answering is not which side you land on but what you found yourself weighing, because that is the bit that is actually about you. Two people can choose the same option for completely opposite reasons, and the reasons are far more interesting than the vote.
之所以差得不多，是因为这种形状的问题在构造时，就让两边都有真实的道理；如果其中一个明显更好，它就不值得问了。所以回答里有用的部分，不是你落在哪一边，而是你发现自己在权衡什么，因为那才是真正关于你的部分。两个人可以出于完全相反的理由选同一个选项，而理由比投票有意思得多。

What made me think about it this way was hearing two friends answer one of these identically and then explain themselves. One had chosen it because it was the safer option and one because it was the riskier one — they had read the same choice in opposite directions. Neither was wrong about the facts. They just disagreed about which side the risk was on, and I would never have discovered that from the answers alone.
让我这样想的，是我听两个朋友对同一个这类问题给出了一样的答案，然后各自解释。一个人选它是因为那是更安全的选项，另一个选它是因为那是更冒险的——他们把同一个选择读成了相反的方向。两人对事实的判断都没错，他们只是在“风险在哪一边”上意见不同；而光看答案，我永远不会发现这一点。
So I will commit to the first one, and I would rather spend the conversation on what nearly tipped me the other way than on defending the choice itself.
所以我会明确地选第一个，而且比起为这个选择辩护，我更愿意把这场对话花在“差一点让我倒向另一边的是什么”上。

open: The honest answer is the one I would not have given five years ago, which is probably why it is worth saying. My first instinct is always to reach for something impressive, and the true answer is usually smaller and more specific than that.
最诚实的答案，是我五年前不会给出的那个，也正因为这样它才值得说。我的第一反应总是想找一个听起来体面的说法，而真实的答案通常比那个更小、更具体。

The reason I have learned to distrust the impressive answer is that it tells you what I would like to be true about myself rather than what is. Anybody can name the admirable version. What actually says something is the detail you would not have chosen — the thing that is true whether or not it makes you look good, and that you notice only because it keeps coming up.
我之所以学会怀疑那个体面的答案，是因为它说的是我希望别人认为我是什么样的人，而不是我实际是什么样的人。那个值得赞许的版本谁都说得出来。真正能说明问题的，是你不会主动挑出来的那个细节——不管它让你显得好不好看，它都是真的，而你之所以注意到它，只是因为它一再出现。

Take last month. I had a free Saturday, no plans, nobody expecting anything from me, and I had been telling people for a year that what I wanted was more time. What I actually did with it was reorganise a cupboard and go for a long walk on my own. Not the ambitious thing I would have described if you had asked me in advance. And it was genuinely one of the better days I have had this year, which told me something I had been getting wrong about what I want.
就说上个月吧。我有一个完全空着的周六，没有安排，也没有人等我做什么，而我已经跟别人说了一年，说我想要的就是多一点时间。结果我拿那一天做的事，是整理了一个柜子，然后一个人走了很久的路。完全不是我事先被问到时会描述的那种有志气的事。而那却是我今年过得最好的日子之一，这让我意识到，我对自己想要什么的判断，一直有点偏差。

So when somebody asks me a question like this I try to answer from what I actually did rather than from what I would like to say. It is less flattering and it is far more interesting, and in my experience it is also the version that gets a real reply rather than a polite one.
所以现在别人问我这类问题，我会尽量从我实际做过的事里回答，而不是从我希望自己怎么说里回答。这样说出来没那么好听，但有意思得多。而且据我的经验，这个版本得到的是真正的回应，而不是一句客气话。
yesno: Yes — though I want to qualify that straight away, because the flat yes would be misleading and the interesting part is the exception.
是的——不过我想马上补充一句，因为光说“是”会让人误解，而有意思的部分恰恰在那个例外里。

The reason I can answer so quickly is that this is one of the few things about myself I have actually tested rather than assumed. Most of what people believe about their own habits is a story they tell rather than something they have checked, and I have been wrong about myself often enough to have stopped trusting the story. This one I have watched closely enough to be confident about, and what I found was not quite what I expected going in.
我之所以能这么快回答，是因为这是少数几件我真的验证过、而不是想当然的关于自己的事。大多数人对自己习惯的看法，是讲给自己听的一个故事，而不是真正检验过的东西；而我对自己判断错的次数够多了，多到不再相信那个故事。这一件我观察得够久，所以有把握，而我发现的结果和我一开始预想的并不太一样。

What settled it was a stretch of about two months last year where circumstances forced the opposite on me — I had no choice in the matter for about eight weeks. I expected to adapt and I did not. By the third week I could feel it in how I was sleeping and how short I was with people, and by the time things went back to normal the difference was obvious to somebody who does not usually notice that sort of thing. That was more convincing than any amount of thinking about it would have been.
让我确定下来的，是去年有大概两个月，情况逼着我过了相反的日子——有八个星期我根本没得选。我以为自己会适应，结果并没有。到第三个星期，我从睡眠和对人说话的耐心上就能感觉出来；等一切恢复正常，连平时不太注意这类事的人都看得出区别。这比我想多久都更有说服力。

So it is a yes, with the qualification that I only know it because I once had it taken away. I would not have been able to answer honestly before that — I would have guessed, and I would have guessed wrong.
所以答案是肯定的，但前提是：我之所以知道，是因为它曾经被拿走过。在那之前我没法诚实地回答——我只能猜，而且会猜错。

open: What I want is much less specific than it used to be, and I have stopped treating that as a failure to have a plan.
我想要的东西比以前具体得多得多——更准确地说，是模糊得多——而我已经不再把这当成“没有计划”的失败。

The reason is that every specific goal I set in my twenties either got reached and turned out not to change much, or got overtaken by something I could not have predicted. Neither outcome was a disaster, but both taught me that I am not a good forecaster of what will make a future version of me satisfied. What I can do reasonably well is notice what a good week currently looks like, and aim at having more of those, which sounds vague and is actually far more testable.
原因是，我二十多岁定下的每一个具体目标，要么达成了却发现没改变多少，要么被一件我根本预测不到的事超越了。两种结果都不算灾难，但都教会了我：对于“什么能让未来的那个我满意”，我不是一个好的预测者。我还算做得不错的，是注意到目前一个好的星期长什么样，然后瞄准“多来几个这样的星期”。这听起来含糊，实际上可检验得多。

The concrete version is that about two years ago I stopped writing down what I wanted to achieve and started writing down, at the end of a good week, what had made it good. After about six months there was an obvious pattern in it that I would not have guessed in advance — almost every entry involved finishing something and almost none involved recognition. That has shaped what I have said yes to since more than any five-year plan ever did.
具体的做法是：大概两年前，我不再写下我想达成什么，而开始在一个好星期结束时写下，是什么让它变好的。大概半年之后，里面出现了一个我事先绝对猜不到的明显规律——几乎每一条都涉及“把某件事做完了”，而几乎没有一条涉及被认可。这件事对我之后答应什么的影响，超过我做过的任何五年计划。
So my answer is that I aim at conditions rather than outcomes now. It is a less impressive thing to say out loud and it has produced better decisions.
所以我的回答是：我现在瞄准的是条件，而不是结果。这话说出来没那么体面，但它带来了更好的决定。

What I would say is that the thing which actually moved the needle for me was not any of the things I spent years reading about — it was sleep, and I resisted that conclusion for a long time because it is so boring.
我会说，真正对我起了作用的，不是我读了好多年的那些东西，而是睡眠。而我抗拒这个结论抗拒了很久，因为它实在太无聊了。

The reason I resisted is that sleep is not a project. You cannot optimise it in an interesting way, there is nothing to buy, and improving it mostly means giving things up rather than adding things. Everything else in this area comes with equipment, a plan and a community, which makes it far more attractive to somebody who likes starting projects. It took me an embarrassingly long time to notice that I was choosing interventions by how engaging they were rather than by whether they worked.
我之所以抗拒，是因为睡眠不是一个项目。你没法用有意思的方式去优化它，没有东西可买，而且改善它主要意味着放弃一些事，而不是增加一些事。这个领域里其他所有东西都配有装备、计划和社群，这对一个喜欢开新项目的人来说吸引力大得多。我花了很不好意思承认的时间才注意到：我一直是按“有不有趣”在挑做法，而不是按“有没有用”。

What settled it was about six weeks where, for unrelated reasons, I was in bed by eleven every night. I had not set out to test anything. By the third week two people had asked me independently whether something good had happened, which was not a question I had been getting. Nothing else had changed — same work, same exercise, same everything. That was more persuasive than any amount of reading, because I had not been trying to prove it.
让我确定下来的，是大概六个星期里，因为一些不相干的原因，我每天十一点前就上床了。我并没有打算验证什么。到第三个星期，有两个人分别问我是不是有什么好事发生了，而这不是我平时会被问到的问题。别的什么都没变——一样的工作、一样的运动、一样的一切。这比读多少东西都更有说服力，因为我当时并不是在试图证明它。
So my honest answer is that I would put every hour I have spent on the interesting parts of this subject into the dull one, if I could have it back.
所以我诚实的回答是：如果能把时间要回来，我会把花在这个话题里所有有趣部分上的每一个小时，都投到那个无聊的部分上去。
yesno: Yes, but not for the reason I would have given a few years ago, and the shift in reasoning matters more to me than the answer.
是的，但原因和我几年前会给的不一样；而这个理由上的转变，对我来说比答案本身更重要。

I used to do it for a result — a number, an appearance, some target I had set. That works for about four months and then stops, because a target is either reached, at which point the motivation goes, or not reached, at which point it goes anyway. What actually made it stick was noticing that I am measurably worse company on days I have not moved at all, and that this was visible to other people before it was visible to me.
我以前是为了一个结果去做的——一个数字、一个外形、我给自己定的某个目标。那种做法能撑大概四个月然后就停了，因为目标要么达成了，动力随之消失；要么没达成，动力照样消失。真正让它坚持下来的，是我注意到：在完全没动过的日子里，我明显是个更难相处的人，而且这一点别人比我先看出来。

The evidence was fairly blunt. There was a winter where I did essentially nothing for about ten weeks, for ordinary reasons — dark, busy, no particular decision involved. Nothing dramatic happened, but I was noticeably shorter with people, and somebody I live with mentioned it before I had connected it to anything. When I started again the difference showed up within a fortnight, and it showed up in my temper long before it showed up anywhere I could photograph.
证据相当直白。有一个冬天，我基本上十个星期什么都没做，原因很平常——天黑、忙、并没有什么特别的决定。也没发生什么戏剧性的事，但我对人明显没了耐心，而和我住在一起的人在我把这件事和任何原因联系起来之前就提了出来。等我重新开始，差别在两个星期之内就出现了，而且它出现在我的脾气上，远早于出现在任何拍得下来的地方。

So it is a yes, and the useful part is that it now has nothing to do with how I look. It is maintenance of something I use every day, which turns out to be a far more durable reason than any target I ever set.
所以答案是肯定的。而有用的部分是：它现在和我的外表毫无关系。它是对一样我每天都在用的东西的维护，而这个理由被证明比我定过的任何目标都耐用得多。

open: I have two that have actually survived more than a year, and I have stopped counting anything as a hobby until it has lasted a full winter.
我有两个真正坚持了一年以上的爱好，而且我现在不会把任何事算作爱好，除非它撑过了一整个冬天。

The reason for that test is that enthusiasm is cheap in September and worthless by February. I have started six or seven things with genuine excitement and finished one. What the ones that lasted have in common is that an evening spent on either leaves something behind — a meal that existed, a route I now know. Office work rarely does that: I can put in nine hours and struggle to name what changed. I think I need the evidence more than I need the activity.
我用这个标准，是因为热情在九月很便宜，到二月就一文不值了。我带着真心的兴奋开始过六七件事，只完成了一件。留下来的那两件的共同点是：一个晚上花在上面，结束之后都能留下点什么——一顿确实存在过的饭，一条我现在认识的路线。办公室的工作很少有这种感觉：我可以干九个小时，却说不出到底改变了什么。我想比起活动本身，我更需要的是那个证据。

The clearest case is cooking, and specifically one dish I spent about a month getting right by making it badly four times in a row. I called my mother after the fourth attempt and she said it smelled correct down the phone, which is obviously not possible, but I knew what she meant. I have made it a dozen times since and written the recipe down properly for the first time in the family, which is more than any of my more ambitious projects have produced.
最清楚的例子是做饭，具体说是一道菜，我花了大概一个月才做对，方法是连着做砸四次。第四次之后我给我妈打电话，她说隔着电话都闻得到那个味道对了——这当然不可能，但我明白她的意思。从那以后我又做了十几次，而且第一次把这个方子认真写了下来，我们家以前没人写过。这比我那些更有志气的项目产出的都多。

So my answer is that my hobbies are whatever produces evidence that the evening happened. That is why those two stuck and the others did not — not because they are more interesting, but because they leave a mark.
所以我的回答是：我的爱好，就是那些能留下证据、证明那个晚上确实存在过的事。这就是为什么那两件留了下来，而别的没有——不是因为它们更有意思，而是因为它们会留下痕迹。
I would give the short version first and let the other person choose which part to open, rather than deciding for them which bit of my background is interesting.
我会先给简短的版本，然后让对方去挑他想打开哪一部分，而不是替他决定我的背景里哪一段有意思。

The reason is that the full version is a paragraph and nobody wants a paragraph thirty seconds into meeting somebody. But the very short version — where I am, roughly what I do — gives the other person nothing to work with either. What seems to work is two or three sentences with slightly uneven edges in them, so there is an obvious place to ask a follow-up if they want one and an easy exit if they do not.
原因是，完整的版本是一整段话，而没有人想在刚认识三十秒的时候听一整段话。但极短的版本——我在哪儿、大概做什么——同样没给对方留下任何可以着手的东西。看起来有效的做法是两三句话，边缘留得稍微不齐，这样对方想追问的话有一个明显的地方可以问，不想问的话也有一个轻松的出口。

The specific thing I have learned is to include one detail that does not fit the rest. If everything in an introduction points the same way it reads as a summary and gets a summary in return. If there is one element that seems out of place — a job that does not match the subject I studied, a city I lived in for a year for no obvious reason — that is almost always what the other person picks up, and the conversation starts there rather than at the beginning.
我具体学到的一点是：加进一个和其余部分不搭的细节。如果一段自我介绍里所有内容都指向同一个方向，它读起来就像一份摘要，换回来的也是一份摘要。而如果其中有一个元素看起来不太对位——一份和所学专业不匹配的工作，一座没有明显理由住了一年的城市——那几乎总是对方会接住的东西，谈话就从那里开始，而不是从头开始。
So my approach is short, with a loose thread left hanging deliberately. It has a considerably better hit rate than either the paragraph or the one-liner, and it lets the other person steer.
所以我的做法是：说得短，但故意留一根松着的线头。它的命中率比那一整段和那一句话都高得多，而且它让对方来掌舵。

yesno: Yes, and I can date it, which is unusual for me — most of my memories have lost their timestamps but this one kept its.
有，而且我能说出具体日期，这对我来说不寻常——我的记忆大多丢了时间戳，只有这一段留着。

The reason it stayed is that it was the first time I noticed something about myself while it was still happening rather than months afterwards. Nearly everything I understand about my own life I understood late, in retrospect, once the situation was safely over. This one I caught live, and something about catching it live pinned the whole day in place. I can still tell you what the weather was doing.
它之所以留下来，是因为那是我第一次在事情还在发生的时候，就注意到了关于自己的某件事，而不是几个月之后才反应过来。我对自己人生的理解，几乎全都是迟到的、事后的，是在局面安全地结束之后才明白的。这一次我是当场抓住的，而“当场抓住”这件事本身，把那一整天钉在了原地。我到现在还能告诉你那天天气怎么样。

It was a Thursday in the autumn, and I had spent about two hours doing something I had been dreading for a fortnight — a conversation, as it happens, that I had rehearsed so many times it had stopped resembling anything I would actually say. It went nothing like the rehearsal. It took eleven minutes. And walking back afterwards I remember thinking, quite clearly, that I had just spent two weeks being frightened of eleven minutes, and that this was almost certainly a pattern rather than a one-off. It was.
那是秋天的一个星期四，我用了大概两个小时，去做一件我已经怕了两个星期的事——碰巧是一场谈话，而我在心里排练了太多遍，练到它已经不像任何我真会说出口的话了。实际过程和排练毫无关系，一共十一分钟。之后走回去的路上，我记得自己非常清楚地想：我刚刚花了两个星期，去害怕十一分钟；而这几乎肯定是一个模式，不是一次意外。后来证明确实是。

So yes — and what makes it worth keeping is not the event, which was minor, but that it is the first time I watched myself do something and understood it in the moment. I have had maybe four of those, and I can date all four.
所以答案是有。而它值得留着的原因不是那件事本身——那件事很小——而是我第一次看着自己做一件事，并且当场就明白了它。这样的时刻我大概只有四次，而这四次我都说得出日期。
open: The one I come back to is not the biggest thing that has happened to me, which surprised me when I worked out that it was the one I kept returning to.
我反复想起的那一段，并不是我人生中最大的事。当我意识到自己一再回到的是它时，我自己也很意外。

The reason, I think, is that big events arrive with a ready-made meaning attached. Somebody dies, somebody is born, you move country — the significance is handed to you and there is not much for you to do with it except feel the appropriate thing. The memories that stay live are the ones nobody told you were important, so you are still working out why they stuck, and a memory you are still working on does not fade.
我想原因是：大事到来的时候，意义是随附在上面的。有人去世、有人出生、你搬到另一个国家——它的分量是被交到你手上的，你能做的不多，只能感受该感受的东西。真正活着的记忆，是那些没人告诉过你它重要的记忆，所以你到现在还在琢磨它为什么留了下来；而一段你还在琢磨的记忆是不会褪色的。

Mine is an ordinary afternoon when I was about nineteen, sitting on a wall outside a building waiting for somebody who was late, with nothing to do and no phone worth looking at. Maybe forty minutes. I remember the specific quality of being completely unoccupied and not minding — no sense that I should be elsewhere, no list running in the background. I have chased that state deliberately for fifteen years since and reached it perhaps a dozen times. At the time I did not know it was rare.
我的那段是十九岁左右一个很普通的下午，我坐在一栋楼外面的矮墙上，等一个迟到的人，没事可做，手机也没什么好看的，大概四十分钟。我记得那种“完全没有事情占着、而且一点也不在意”的具体质感——没有觉得自己应该在别处，脑子后台也没有清单在跑。之后这十五年我一直有意识地追这个状态，大概只到达过十来次。而当时我并不知道它有多稀有。

So what I would say is that the memories worth keeping are rarely the ones you would put in an account of your life. They are the ones that turned out to be the baseline you have been measuring against ever since, and you usually do not find out which those are until much later.
所以我会说：值得保留的记忆，很少是你会写进人生简介里的那些。它们是那些后来变成基准线的东西——你从那以后一直拿它在衡量别的一切——而通常你要很久以后才知道，哪些是那样的记忆。
The thing I would say is that the decisions that actually mattered were all small and recurring, and none of them were the ones I spent time thinking about.
我会说：真正起作用的决定，全都是小而重复的；而它们没有一个是我花时间去想的那些。

The reason is that large financial decisions are rare, obvious and get all the attention, while the things that determine the shape of a year are the ones repeating quietly in the background. I spent a great deal of energy in my twenties on the big infrequent choices and almost none on the small automatic ones, and looking back the automatic ones account for nearly all the difference.
原因是，大额的财务决定罕见、显眼、拿走了全部注意力；而决定一整年形态的，是那些在背景里安静重复的东西。我二十多岁把大量精力花在那些少见的大选择上，几乎没有花在那些小的、自动的选择上；而回头看，几乎全部差别都来自那些自动的部分。

The clearest case is that about three years ago I went through everything leaving my account monthly and cancelled a third of it in an afternoon. Not because any single item was significant — most were small enough that I had never questioned them — but because collectively they added up to something I would not have agreed to if it had been presented as one number. The exercise took perhaps ninety minutes and its effect over three years is larger than any single decision I have made in this area.
最清楚的一次是大概三年前，我把每个月从账户里出去的所有款项过了一遍，用一个下午取消了其中三分之一。不是因为哪一项数额显著——大多数小到我从来没质疑过——而是因为它们加在一起，是一个如果一开始就以单一数字呈现给我、我绝不会同意的金额。这件事大概花了九十分钟，而它三年下来的效果，比我在这个领域做过的任何单一决定都大。

So my answer is that the useful discipline is not restraint at the point of purchase, it is periodically looking at the total. The individual decisions are almost always defensible; it is only the sum that tells you anything.
所以我的答案是：有用的自律不在付款的那一刻克制，而在于定期去看那个总数。单独的每一个决定几乎总是说得通的，只有加总才告诉你一些东西。

opinion: My position is yes in principle, and I am much less confident about the version of it that usually gets proposed — which I realise is an unsatisfying way to start, but the gap between those two things is where the actual argument lives.
我的立场是：原则上赞成，但对通常被提出来的那个具体版本，我的信心要低得多。我知道这样开头不太痛快，但真正的争论就在这两者之间的缝隙里。

The reason I separate them is that most disagreements I have had about questions like this turned out not to be about the principle at all. Almost everybody agrees on the principle when it is stated broadly enough. What people disagree about is who pays, who decides, and what happens to the cases the rule was not written for — and those are the parts that get skipped when the question is asked in the abstract.
我之所以把它们分开，是因为我在这类问题上有过的大多数分歧，最后都发现根本不是关于原则的。只要说得足够宽泛，几乎所有人都同意那个原则。人们真正分歧的是：谁付代价、谁来决定，以及那些规则当初没考虑到的情况怎么办——而这些恰恰是问题被抽象地提出来时会被跳过的部分。

The example that taught me this was an argument I had a few years ago where I was certain I disagreed with somebody, and after about forty minutes it turned out we agreed completely on what should happen and disagreed only about who should be responsible for making it happen. Forty minutes to find that out. I had been arguing against a position she did not hold, and she had been doing the same to me, and neither of us noticed because we had both been arguing at the level of the principle.
教会我这一点的，是几年前的一次争论。我当时确信我和对方意见相反，结果吵了大概四十分钟才发现：我们对“应该发生什么”完全一致，只在“谁该负责让它发生”上有分歧。花了四十分钟才弄清楚这个。我一直在反对一个她并不持有的立场，她对我也一样，而我们谁都没察觉，因为我们都在原则那一层上争论。
So my answer is a qualified yes, and I would rather be asked the narrower version of the question. The broad one produces agreement that dissolves the moment anything has to actually be decided.
所以我的答案是有保留的赞成，而且我更希望被问到那个更窄的版本。宽泛的那个问题制造出来的一致，一到真要做决定的时候就会溶解。
open: The thing I would point at is not the loudest problem, it is the one that almost nobody argues about because it looks like the weather rather than a decision.
我会指出的不是声音最大的那个问题，而是几乎没有人在争论的那个——因为它看起来像天气，而不像一个决定。

The reason those are the ones worth naming is that anything being publicly argued over is already receiving attention, and attention is most of what fixing something requires. The genuinely stuck problems are the ones everybody has quietly accepted as background conditions — the things you would have to point out to somebody before they could even see them as changeable. Once something is treated as simply how things are, no amount of it getting worse produces a response.
这类问题之所以值得点出来，是因为任何正在被公开争论的事，已经获得了注意力，而注意力本身就是解决问题所需要的大部分东西。真正卡住的问题，是那些所有人都默默接受为背景条件的东西——你得先指给一个人看，他才可能意识到那是可以改变的。一旦某件事被当成“事情本来就是这样”，那么它再怎么恶化，也不会引起反应。

The specific case I would give is small enough to sound trivial, which is exactly the point: the assumption that being reachable at all hours is part of an ordinary job. Nobody decided that. There was no policy, no announcement, no debate — it arrived with the technology and was absorbed within about a decade, and it is now so normal that objecting to it sounds eccentric rather than reasonable. A generation ago it would have been an extraordinary demand.
我要举的具体例子小到听起来微不足道，而这恰恰是重点：那个“随时能被找到是一份普通工作的一部分”的假设。没有人做过这个决定。没有政策、没有公告、没有辩论——它跟着技术一起到来，在十年左右的时间里被吸收，而现在它正常到反对它听起来像是古怪，而不是合理。放在一代人以前，这会是一个极其过分的要求。

So what I would say is that the things worth examining are the ones that never got argued about. Anything with two sides already has people working on it. It is the settled questions that are usually the ones that were never actually asked.
所以我会说：值得审视的，恰恰是那些从来没被争论过的事。任何有两方立场的问题，已经有人在处理了；反而是那些被当成定论的问题，通常是从来没有真正被提出来过的。
The description I would give of myself now is narrower and less flattering than the one I would have given at twenty-five, and I think that is progress rather than decline.
我现在会给自己的描述，比二十五岁时的那个更窄，也更不好听，而我认为这是进步，不是退步。

The reason is that most self-description is aspiration in disguise. At twenty-five I would have listed qualities I admired and quietly assumed I had them, because nothing had yet tested whether I did. Ten more years of being observably myself in front of other people has cut that list down considerably, and what is left is a smaller number of things I can actually demonstrate rather than claim.
原因是，大多数自我描述其实是伪装成描述的愿望。二十五岁的我会列出一堆我欣赏的品质，然后默默假设自己拥有它们，因为当时还没有任何事情检验过我到底有没有。之后又当了十年“被别人看在眼里的自己”，这份清单被砍掉了一大截，剩下的是数量少得多、但我能拿出来演示而不只是声称的东西。

The specific one I would name is that I am much better at starting things than finishing them, and I have stopped calling that enthusiasm. I have three notebooks with excellent first twenty pages. I have learned two instruments to the point of being able to play badly and no further. Last year I counted the projects I had begun and abandoned in the previous eighteen months and the number was nine, which is not a personality quirk, it is a pattern with a cost. Since then I have started saying no to new things while something is still open, which works about half the time.
我会具体说出来的那一条是：我开始一件事的能力远强于把它做完的能力，而我已经不再把这叫作有热情了。我有三个本子，前二十页都写得非常好。我学过两种乐器，学到能弹得很难听为止，再没往前。去年我数了一下前十八个月里开了头又放弃的项目，一共九个——这就不是什么性格上的小怪癖了，这是一个有代价的模式。从那以后，只要手上还有没结的事，我就开始对新的说不，大概一半的时候管用。

So the honest description is one real strength, one real weakness I can prove with examples, and much less certainty about the rest than I used to have. It is a less impressive answer and a considerably more useful one.
所以诚实的描述是：一个真实的长处、一个我能用例子证明的真实短处，以及对其余部分远比从前少的把握。这个答案没那么体面，但有用得多。
yesno: Yes, though I would have said no about five years ago, and the change is the interesting part rather than the answer.
是的，不过五年前我会说不是；有意思的地方在那个变化，而不在答案本身。

The reason I would have said no is that I was describing the person I was in the settings I found easy. In a room of three people I have always been one way; in a room of thirty I am reliably another, and for years I answered questions like this from whichever version had been in charge most recently. Once I noticed that, the honest answer stopped being a single word and became a question about context — which is less satisfying to say and much closer to true.
我当年会说“不是”的原因是：我描述的是我在自己觉得轻松的场合里的那个人。在三个人的房间里我一直是一种样子，在三十个人的房间里我稳定地是另一种；而有好些年，我回答这类问题，用的都是最近一次当家的那个版本。意识到这一点之后，诚实的答案就不再是一个词，而变成了一个关于场合的问题——这样说没那么痛快，但离真实近得多。

What made it visible was a job about four years ago that put me in front of large groups every week for eight months. I expected to hate it and I did, for roughly six weeks. Then it became ordinary, and by the end I was doing it without the preceding two hours of dread. Nothing about me changed underneath — I still leave those rooms wanting silence — but the observable behaviour changed completely, and to everybody watching that is the same thing as the trait changing.
让这件事变得可见的，是四年前的一份工作，它让我连着八个月每周都要站在很多人面前。我以为自己会讨厌它，事实上我确实讨厌了大概六个星期。然后它就变成了日常，到最后我做这件事之前，不再需要先害怕两个小时。我身上底下的东西一点没变——我离开那种房间时依然只想要安静——但可观察到的行为完全变了；而对所有旁观的人来说，这和这个性格特征本身变了是一回事。
So my answer is yes, in most settings, most of the time, and I have made my peace with the fact that this kind of question can only really be answered with conditions attached.
所以我的回答是：在大多数场合、大多数时候，是的。而我也接受了一件事：这类问题真正诚实的回答，一定是要附带条件的。

open: What I look for now is much simpler than what I looked for at twenty, and it is basically one thing: does this person ask me questions back.
我现在找的东西，比二十岁时找的简单得多，基本只有一条：这个人会不会反过来问我问题。

The reason it has narrowed to that is that everything else I used to weigh — shared interests, similar background, liking the same things — turned out to predict almost nothing about whether a friendship would survive. I have lost touch with people I had a great deal in common with, and I am still close to two people I agree with about almost nothing. The variable that actually held was curiosity, in both directions, sustained over years.
之所以收窄到这一条，是因为我以前掂量的其他因素——共同爱好、相似的背景、喜欢同样的东西——事实证明几乎无法预测一段友谊能不能活下来。我和一些跟我共同点极多的人已经失去联系，却和两个几乎在任何事上都和我看法不同的人一直很近。真正起作用的变量是好奇心，双向的，而且要能维持很多年。

The friendship that proves it is one where we have essentially no overlapping interests. Different work, different taste in almost everything, and when we meet we spend the first twenty minutes catching up on things neither of us follows. What we do have is a habit, which started as a joke, of asking each other what we have changed our minds about lately. Ten years of that question has produced more genuine conversation than a decade of shared hobbies would have, and it is the only thing I would say we deliberately do.
能证明这一点的，是一段我们几乎没有任何交集的友谊。工作不同，几乎所有品味都不同，见面时前二十分钟都在补对方那边我们完全不关注的事。我们真正共有的是一个习惯，一开始是当玩笑的：互相问对方最近改变了什么想法。这一个问题问了十年，产生的真实对话，比十年共同爱好能产生的多得多，而这也是我们唯一有意识在做的事。
So my social style, if I have one, is that I have stopped trying to find people like me and started noticing who is actually interested. It is a much shorter list and it has held up far better.
所以要说我的社交方式，那就是：我不再试图找和我相似的人，而开始注意谁是真的感兴趣。这份名单短得多，也稳固得多。
yesno: Yes, but much less than I used to, and the reduction was deliberate rather than something that happened to me.
是的，不过比以前少了很多，而且这个减少是我有意为之，不是自然而然发生的。

The reason I cut it back is that I was treating the number of people I saw as evidence of something, without ever asking what. I would end a busy week feeling like I had done social life correctly, and also feeling that I had not had a single conversation I could recall on the Monday. That is a lot of hours for no return. At some point I worked out that I was optimising for the count rather than for anything that happens inside the count.
我之所以砍下来，是因为我一直把见过多少人当成某种证明，却从来没问过是证明什么。我会在一个很忙的星期结束时，觉得自己“社交生活做对了”，同时又发现到周一想不起任何一场谈话。这么多小时，回报是零。到某个时候我才想明白，我优化的是数量本身，而不是数量里面真正发生的东西。

So about three years ago I stopped agreeing to things by default. The concrete change was small: I started saying I would check and reply tomorrow rather than saying yes in the moment, which puts a day of friction exactly where there had been none. My social calendar roughly halved within four months. What I noticed after that is that the conversations got longer, because I was no longer moving on to the next thing, and I saw three or four people considerably more rather than a dozen people occasionally.
所以大概三年前，我不再默认答应任何邀约。具体的改动很小：我开始说“我看一下，明天回复你”，而不是当场说好，这恰恰在原本一点摩擦都没有的地方，加进了一天的摩擦。四个月之内，我的社交安排大概少了一半。之后我注意到，谈话变长了，因为我不再急着赶去下一个地方；而且我见三四个人的次数明显变多，而不是偶尔见十几个人。
So the answer is yes, with the size of it now chosen rather than accumulated. That is the part I would defend — not the number, but the fact that it is a decision.
所以答案是肯定的，只是它的规模现在是被选出来的，而不是堆积出来的。我要辩护的正是这一点——不是那个数字，而是它是一个决定。

open: What I would say is that the thing animals gave me as a child was not companionship in the way people usually mean — it was being the person something else depended on.
我会说：小时候动物给我的，不是大家通常说的那种陪伴，而是“成为另一个生命所依赖的那个人”。

The reason that mattered is that a child is otherwise entirely on the receiving end of care. Everything is done for you and nothing is done by you, and being the one an animal comes to when it is hungry is the first reversal of that most people get. My parents were quite deliberate about handing me the feeding rather than doing it themselves, which at the time felt like a chore and in hindsight was obviously the point.
这之所以重要，是因为一个孩子在其他所有方面都处在接受照顾的那一端。一切都是别人替你做的，没有一件是你做的；而当一只动物饿了会来找你，这是大多数人得到的第一次反转。我父母相当有意识地把喂食这件事交给我，而不是自己做；当时我只觉得是个麻烦事，现在回头看，那显然就是重点。

The specific case was a cat we had for fourteen years. She arrived when I was eight and died when I was twenty-two, so she was there for essentially every part of my life I can remember properly. She was in the room when I did my exams. At the end she was deaf and slept on the warm bit of floor by the radiator, and my father — who had spent fourteen years announcing that he was not a cat person — was the one who sat with her.
具体的例子是我们养了十四年的一只猫。她来我们家的时候我八岁，走的时候我二十二岁，也就是说，我能清楚记得的人生阶段，她几乎全程都在。我考试的时候她在房间里。到最后她耳朵聋了，喜欢睡在暖气旁边地板发热的那一块；而我父亲——那个用了十四年宣布自己不喜欢猫的人——是最后陪着她的那个。

So I do not really think of her as a pet in memory. She is closer to a measuring stick: the constant across everything that changed between eight and twenty-two, and I notice I still date things by her without meaning to.
所以在记忆里我不太把她当成宠物。她更像一把尺子：从八岁到二十二岁，别的都在变，只有她是不变的那一个。我发现自己到现在还会不自觉地拿她来给事情标记时间。

opinion: I hold a position on this, and I hold it a good deal less confidently than I would have ten years ago, which I have come to think is the more important half of the answer.
我在这件事上有立场，而且我持有它的把握，比十年前小得多。我逐渐认为，这后半句才是答案里更重要的那一半。

The reason is that I noticed my views in this area correlated far too neatly with the views of the people I spend time with. That is not evidence that they are wrong, but it is evidence that I did not arrive at them by the route I thought I did. Once you see that pattern in yourself it is difficult to unsee, and it has made me much more interested in why somebody disagrees than in whether I can defeat them, which is a slower and considerably less satisfying way to have a conversation.
原因是，我注意到自己在这个领域的看法，和我常来往的人的看法吻合得过于整齐。这不能证明那些看法是错的，但足以证明我并不是通过我以为的那条路得出它们的。一旦你在自己身上看见这个规律，就很难再装作没看见；而它让我对“为什么有人不同意”远比对“我能不能驳倒他”更感兴趣——这是一种慢得多、也没那么痛快的聊天方式。

The thing that produced the shift was making myself read a long, serious argument for a position I found obviously wrong — not a caricature of it, the best version I could find. I did not change my mind. But I came out understanding that the disagreement was about a genuine trade-off with real costs on both sides, rather than about one group being foolish. That is a small change and it altered how I talk about the subject completely.
促成这个转变的，是我逼自己读了一篇很长、很认真的文章，为一个我认为显然错误的立场辩护——不是它的漫画版，而是我能找到的最好的版本。我没有改变主意。但读完之后我明白了：这个分歧关乎一个真实的取舍，两边都有实实在在的代价，而不是某一群人愚蠢。这是一个很小的变化，却彻底改变了我谈论这个话题的方式。
So my answer includes the position and the confidence level, because I think stating the second is the part that makes the conversation possible at all.
所以我的回答里既包含立场，也包含我对它的把握程度。因为我认为，说出后者才是让这场对话有可能进行下去的那部分。
open: What I would change first is not the policy anybody argues about — it is the fact that almost nothing in this area is ever measured after it is done.
我最先想改的，不是任何人在争论的那项政策，而是这个领域里几乎没有任何东西在实施之后被衡量过。

The reason I would start there is that without measurement every argument stays an argument forever. Two sides predict opposite outcomes, something is implemented, and then nobody checks. Five years later both sides are still making the same predictions with the same confidence, because nothing has happened that could have proved either of them wrong. That is not a disagreement about values, it is a system that cannot learn, and it makes the value disagreements much harder than they need to be.
我之所以从这里开始，是因为没有衡量，每一场争论就会永远停留在争论。两边预测相反的结果，某件事被实施了，然后没有人去核对。五年之后，两边还在用同样的把握做同样的预测，因为从来没有发生任何能证明其中一方错了的事。这不是价值观上的分歧，这是一个学不会的系统；而它让那些真正的价值分歧变得比本来该有的困难得多。

The example that convinced me was watching a fairly major change happen locally where I live — one everybody had strong opinions about beforehand. It went in. Nobody I know can tell me whether it worked, including the people who were loudest about it. There was no follow-up, no published numbers, nothing. Both camps simply carried on believing what they had believed, and the whole exercise produced no information at all.
说服我的例子，是我看着我住的地方发生了一次相当大的变动——一件所有人事先都意见强烈的事。它落地了。而我认识的人里，没有一个能告诉我它到底有没有用，包括当初嗓门最大的那些人。没有回访，没有公布的数据，什么都没有。两边就这样各自继续相信原来相信的东西，整件事没有产生任何信息。

So my answer is a procedural one rather than a political one, and I am aware that makes it a boring answer. But almost everything else I would want depends on it, and none of it is possible while nobody is counting.
所以我的答案是程序性的，而不是政治性的，我也知道这让它变成一个无聊的答案。但我想要的几乎所有其他东西都依赖于它，而在没有人计数的情况下，那些东西一个都不可能实现。

yesno: Yes, and it is one of the few preferences of mine that has held steady long enough that I have stopped expecting it to change.
是的，而且这是我为数不多、稳定得够久、久到我已经不再指望它会改变的偏好之一。

The reason I mention the steadiness is that most of what I would once have called my taste turned out to be a phase with a confident voice. Things I was certain about at twenty-two I find slightly baffling now, and things I would have dismissed then are things I return to weekly. After enough of that you stop treating a current preference as a fact about yourself, and the few that survive a decade start to look genuinely informative by comparison.
我之所以提“稳定”这一点，是因为我从前会称之为品味的东西，大部分后来都被证明只是一个说话很有底气的阶段。二十二岁时我确信不疑的东西，现在看来有点莫名其妙；而那时候我会一口否定的东西，如今我每周都会回去。经历够多这样的事之后，你就不再把当下的偏好当成关于自己的事实；相比之下，那几个撑过十年的，才开始显得真正有信息量。

This one I can date, which is unusual. I know roughly when it started because it began as an obligation — something I did because the situation required it, not because I wanted to — and I remember the point at which I noticed I was choosing it when nothing required me to. That gap, between doing something because you have to and catching yourself doing it freely, is the only reliable evidence I know of that a preference is real rather than performed.
这一个我能说出大致的时间，这不常见。我知道它大概是什么时候开始的，因为它一开始是一种义务——我做它是因为情况需要，不是因为我想要——而我记得那个时刻：我发现自己在没有任何东西要求我的情况下，主动选了它。“因为不得不做”和“撞见自己自愿在做”之间的那道缝，是我所知唯一可靠的证据，能说明一个偏好是真实的而不是表演出来的。
So the answer is yes, and the thing I would actually offer is the test: watch what you do when nobody has asked you to. It is a much better guide than anything you would say about yourself.
所以答案是肯定的。而我真正想提供的是那个检验方法：看看在没有人要求你的时候你做什么。它比你关于自己说的任何话都是更好的指南。

open: What I would say is that I am much more interested in the practices than in the propositions, and that this is where I have ended up rather than where I started.
我会说：我对那些实践的兴趣，远大于对那些命题的兴趣；而这是我最后走到的位置，不是我出发的位置。

The reason is that I spent a long time treating this as a question with a factual answer that I needed to settle before I could do anything else. That turned out to be the wrong shape of question for how it actually operates in people's lives. The people I know for whom it matters most are not, day to day, holding a position — they are doing something regularly, usually with other people, and the belief is downstream of the practice rather than upstream of it.
