原因是，我曾经很长一段时间把这当成一个有事实答案的问题，觉得必须先把它解决掉才能做别的。后来发现，就它在人们生活里实际的运作方式而言，这个问题的形状是错的。我认识的那些最看重这件事的人，在日常里并不是在“持有一个立场”——他们是在定期做某件事，通常和别人一起；而信念是那个实践的下游，不是上游。

What made that visible was going along to something for entirely social reasons, expecting to be a polite observer. What struck me was not any part of the content — it was that a hundred people were doing the same thing at the same time, weekly, for reasons that had nothing to do with productivity, and that almost nothing else in modern life is shaped like that. Whatever else is or is not true, that structure is doing something real, and I had no equivalent of it.
让我看清这一点的，是我完全出于社交理由去参加了一次活动，本来打算当个礼貌的旁观者。让我震动的不是内容的任何部分，而是：一百个人在同一时间做同一件事，每周一次，理由和产出效率毫无关系；而现代生活里几乎没有别的东西是这个形状。不管别的是不是真的，这个结构确实在起某种真实的作用，而我自己没有任何与之对应的东西。
So my answer is that the question I find live is not what people believe but what regular, shared, unproductive thing they do — and I notice that I do not have a good answer to that about myself.
所以我的答案是：我觉得真正活着的问题不是人们相信什么，而是他们定期地、和别人一起地、不为产出地做着什么——而我注意到，关于我自己，我答不好这个问题。
yesno: No, and I want to say that in a way that does not sound like a position I am defending, because I am not particularly invested in it.
不是。而我想用一种听起来不像在捍卫某个立场的方式说出来，因为我对它其实没有太大投入。

The reason I add that is that this subject has a habit of turning into a debate the moment anybody answers it, and the debate is almost always less interesting than what the person actually meant. A flat no from me is a description of where I have ended up, not a claim about where anybody else should be, and I have found that saying so explicitly is the difference between a conversation and an argument.
我之所以补这一句，是因为这个话题有个习惯：只要有人给出答案，它就会立刻变成一场辩论，而那场辩论几乎总是比说话的人真正的意思无趣得多。我给出的这个干脆的“不是”，描述的是我最后走到了哪里，不是在主张别人该在哪里；而我发现，把这一点明说出来，就是一场对话和一场争论之间的区别。

What made me careful about it was a long conversation, some years ago, with somebody whose answer was the opposite of mine. I went in braced for the version of that discussion I had had before, and it did not happen — she was far more interested in what I found difficult about it than in correcting me. About an hour in I realised I had never actually been asked that, only told things, and that I did not have a well-formed answer ready. I have thought about that conversation more than any of the ones where I won.
让我在这件事上变得谨慎的，是若干年前和一个答案与我相反的人的一次长谈。我进去时已经做好了准备，以为会重演我以前经历过的那种讨论，结果并没有——她对“我觉得这件事哪里难”的兴趣，远大于纠正我。大概一个小时之后我意识到：从来没有人这样问过我，别人只是不停地告诉我；而我并没有一个成形的答案。那次对话我想起的次数，比我“赢了”的任何一次都多。
So the answer is no, held without much heat, and I would rather hear how somebody arrived at theirs than compare conclusions.
所以答案是否定的，而且我持有得并不激烈。比起比较结论，我更想听一个人是怎么走到他那个答案的。

open: The thing I would name is a teacher rather than a subject, and specifically one who treated our opinions as things worth arguing with.
我会说出来的是一位老师，而不是一门课，具体说是那位把我们的看法当成值得认真反驳的东西的老师。

The reason that matters is that it sounds like a small distinction and it is not. Most teaching I encountered treated a fourteen-year-old's view as something to be gently corrected on the way to the right answer. He treated it as a position that had to be defended, which meant that having a view suddenly carried a cost, and that changed how carefully we formed them. It is the only thing from that period that has obviously stayed with me.
这一点之所以重要，是因为它听起来是个很小的区别，其实不是。我遇到的大多数教学，会把一个十四岁孩子的观点当成一个需要被温和纠正、然后走向标准答案的东西。而他把它当成一个必须被辩护的立场，这意味着“有一个看法”突然是有代价的，于是我们形成看法时就认真多了。那是那个阶段唯一明显留在我身上的东西。

The lesson everybody in that class still remembers is one where he spent the entire hour letting us dismantle something he had told us the week before. He had given us an explanation; over the weekend two students found material that contradicted it; and rather than tidy that away he handed the hour over. At the end he said, in front of thirty of us, that he had been overconfident about it. I was fifteen and I do not think I had ever seen an adult do that.
那个班上所有人到现在还记得的一节课，是他用整整一节课让我们拆解他上一周告诉我们的东西。他给过我们一个解释；周末有两个同学找到了和它矛盾的材料；他没有把这件事轻轻带过，而是把那节课交了出来。到最后，他当着我们三十个人的面说，他当初对那个说法过于自信了。我那年十五岁，我想我此前没见过一个大人这样做。

So what I took from school was not the content, which I have mostly lost. It was the discovery that a subject can be argued with — and I have since noticed that people who never had that lesson tend to treat their own opinions the same way they were taught to treat facts.
所以我从学校带走的不是知识内容，那些我大多已经忘了，而是一个发现：一门学科是可以被反驳的。后来我注意到，那些从没上过这一课的人，往往用他们被教着对待事实的方式，来对待自己的观点。
yesno: Yes, and the way I would answer it now is almost the opposite of how I would have answered it while I was actually in education.
是的，而我现在回答的方式，几乎和我还在上学时会给的答案相反。

The reason is that I have since learned far more, and far more durably, by being responsible for things I could not yet do than by studying them first. Courses never stuck for me: I have started six or seven and finished one. There is no consequence to stopping in week three, so week three is where I stop. Being answerable to somebody else for a deadline has never once failed to make me learn something, because embarrassment turns out to be a much more reliable motivator than curiosity.
原因是，我后来学到的东西，靠“为我还不会的事负责”得到的，比先去研究它得到的多得多，也牢固得多。上课对我从来没用：我开始过六七门，只学完过一门。第三周停下来没有任何后果，所以第三周就是我停下来的地方。而只要我要对别人的截止时间负责，就没有一次不学会的，因为事实证明，尴尬这个动力比好奇心可靠得多。

The clearest case was about two years ago, when the person who made my team's presentations left and nobody replaced her. I volunteered, largely because the alternative was worse slides. For three months I produced things that were genuinely bad and was told so, politely, most weeks. I learned more about how information should be laid out in that period than from the two books on the subject I had read beforehand and remembered nothing from. The difference is that the books had no Thursday in them.
最清楚的一次是大概两年前，我们组做幻灯片的那个人离职了，也没人接替。我主动接了下来，主要是因为不接的话幻灯片会更难看。有三个月我做出来的东西是真的很差，而且几乎每周都会有人客气地告诉我。那段时间我学到的关于“信息该怎么排布”的东西，比我之前读过的两本相关的书多得多——那两本书我一点都没记住。区别在于，书里没有星期四。

So it is a yes, with the strong qualification that what worked for me was volunteering for the thing I was not qualified for while the stakes were still low enough that being bad at it was survivable.
所以答案是肯定的，但有一个很强的前提：对我有用的做法是，趁着风险还小、做得差还能承受的时候，主动去接那些我还不够格的活儿。

open: What I would say is that almost everything that matters here is about being able to talk about it, rather than about anything else — and that took me until my thirties to work out.
我会说：这方面几乎所有重要的东西，都关乎能不能把它说出来，而不是别的什么；而我到三十多岁才想明白这一点。

The reason is that this is the one area where people are expected to arrive already knowing what they want, and where admitting you are not sure feels like a failure rather than an ordinary state. So the default becomes guessing about each other silently and hoping. That works for a while and then stops working, and when it stops the problem is never really the thing itself, it is that neither of you built any way of raising it.
原因是，这是唯一一个大家默认你到场时就已经知道自己想要什么的领域；而在这里承认自己不确定，感觉像是一种失败，而不是一种普通的状态。于是默认做法就变成了：彼此沉默地猜，然后指望蒙对。这样能维持一阵子，然后就不行了；而它失效的时候，问题从来不真的是那件事本身，而是你们两个谁都没有建立起任何可以提起它的方式。

The clearest thing I have learned came from a conversation that I put off for months and that took, in the end, about fifteen minutes. Fifteen minutes, after months of assuming it would be difficult. What made it possible was that it happened well away from the situation itself — a walk, in daylight, nothing at stake in that moment. I have since noticed that is the general rule: this subject is nearly impossible to discuss in the room it belongs to, and quite easy to discuss almost anywhere else.
我学到的最清楚的一件事，来自一场我拖了好几个月的谈话，而它最后一共花了大概十五分钟。十五分钟，在我假设它会很难之后的好几个月。让它成为可能的是：它发生在离那个情境很远的地方——散步的时候，白天，那一刻没有任何东西悬着。后来我注意到这是个普遍规律：这个话题在它所属的那个房间里几乎无法讨论，而在几乎任何别的地方都相当容易讨论。

So my answer is about timing and setting rather than content. Get the conversation out of the situation and most of the difficulty disappears, which is not advice anybody gave me and is the thing I would pass on.
所以我的答案关乎时机和场合，而不是内容。把这场对话挪出那个情境，大部分困难就消失了。这不是任何人告诉过我的建议，而是我想传下去的那一条。
yesno: Yes, and I would rather answer it plainly than dance around it, because the dancing is usually more awkward than the answer.
是的，而且我宁愿直接回答，也不想绕来绕去，因为绕圈子通常比答案本身更尴尬。

The reason I say that is that questions in this area get their difficulty almost entirely from the run-up. The actual content is generally unremarkable — most people's answers are far more ordinary than the elaborate hedging that precedes them would suggest. What makes the exchange uncomfortable is two people each waiting to see how careful the other is going to be, and both of them escalating the carefulness in response.
我这么说的原因是，这个领域的问题，难度几乎全部来自铺垫。实际内容通常平平无奇——大多数人的答案，比前面那一大堆小心翼翼的铺垫所暗示的要普通得多。让这种交流变得不自在的，是两个人各自等着看对方会有多谨慎，然后互相把谨慎的程度往上加。

I learned that from being on the receiving end of it. Somebody asked me something in this territory, directly, with no preamble and no apology attached, and my first reaction was mild alarm followed almost immediately by relief — because a direct question is much easier to answer than a heavily qualified one. I gave a direct answer back and the whole thing took a minute. Had either of us been careful about it we would have spent ten minutes and said less.
我是从被问的一方学到这一点的。有人在这个范围里直接问了我一件事，没有铺垫，也没有附带道歉；我的第一反应是轻微的警觉，紧接着几乎立刻是松了一口气——因为一个直接的问题，比一个层层限定的问题好回答得多。我也直接回答了他，整件事花了一分钟。如果我们两个谁小心翼翼，我们会花十分钟，而且说得更少。

So the answer is yes, and the more useful observation is that with somebody you have only just met the tone matters far more than the topic. Asked plainly, almost anything is answerable; asked with a lot of preamble, almost nothing is.
所以答案是肯定的。而更有用的观察是：面对刚认识的人，语气远比话题重要。问得直白，几乎什么都能答；铺垫一大堆，几乎什么都答不了。

open: What I would point at is not the sport, it is proximity — I follow one club near where I live and no national side at all, and that surprises people.
我要指出的不是某项运动，而是“距离”——我只关注一支住处附近的球队，完全不关注国家队，而这常常让人意外。

The reason is that following something local means the results actually change the mood of the place you are in. That is a real thing that happens to a street, and it is completely different from watching a televised event involving people you have no connection to. I have also noticed that supporting something successful and distant is a much thinner experience than supporting something ordinary and close, because with the distant one you are only ever consuming the outcome.
原因是，支持一支本地的球队意味着比赛结果会真的改变你所在的地方的气氛。那是一件真实发生在一条街上的事，和看电视里一群和你毫无关系的人比赛完全不同。我还注意到，支持一支成功但遥远的队伍，体验要单薄得多，因为对遥远的那一支，你消费的永远只有结果。

The season before last my club went up, and the thing I remember is not the match. It is walking home afterwards and being able to hear the whole neighbourhood — not a crowd in a stadium, but individual houses, doors open, people out on the pavement who I am fairly sure do not go to games. A woman I have never spoken to said something to me from her doorway. No televised match has ever produced thirty seconds of that.
前年我那支球队升级了，而我记得的不是那场比赛，是赛后走回家的路上，我能听见整个社区的声音——不是体育场里的人群，而是一户一户的人家，门开着，人站在人行道上，其中我相当确定有些人根本不去看球。有个我从没说过话的女士从门口跟我说了句什么。电视转播的比赛从来没有给过我哪怕三十秒这样的东西。
So proximity matters far more to me than the standard of play, and I would rather watch a mediocre event involving people who live twenty minutes away than an excellent one involving strangers.
所以对我来说，离得近比水平高重要得多。我宁愿看一场水平一般、但参赛的人住在二十分钟车程之内的比赛，也不愿看一场精彩但全是陌生人的比赛。

是的，但比以前刻意少了很多；而且我会说，这个减少让我状态更好，而不是消息更闭塞。

The reason is that the constant version was producing anxiety without producing understanding. If you check something every hour, what you get is the same story in eight slightly different states of incompleteness, and your brain files each version as new information when it is not. I also noticed I could tell you what had happened but not why it mattered, which is a strange kind of ignorance to arrive at through effort.
原因是，那种一直看的方式只制造焦虑，不产生理解。如果你每小时刷一次，你得到的是同一件事的八个稍微不同、都不完整的版本，而你的大脑会把每一个版本都归档成新信息，其实并不是。我还注意到，我能告诉你发生了什么，却说不出它为什么重要——靠努力得到这样一种无知，是挺奇怪的。

The change was taking one particular thing off my phone in January. I did it because the phone was full and I was deleting things, which is an unheroic origin for what turned out to be the most useful decision I made that year. I expected consequences and there have been none. Nobody has mentioned it. The test was a holiday in August — nine days away, and I came back to about sixty messages, of which four still needed anything and none had been urgent by the time I read them.
那个改动是我一月份把某样东西从手机上删掉了。我这么做是因为手机存储满了，我在删东西——作为“我那年做过的最有用的决定”的起因，这实在上不了台面。我本来预计会有后果，结果一个都没有。没有人提起过这件事。真正的检验是八月份的假期：出去九天，回来时大概有六十条消息，其中还需要处理的有四条，而且到我看的时候没有一条还是紧急的。
So it is a yes about the activity and a firm no about the frequency, and I would say to anybody considering the same thing that the availability matters far less than you assume.
所以，对这件活动本身我的回答是肯定的，对频率则是坚决否定的。而我想对任何在考虑同样做法的人说：那份“随时可用”远没有你以为的重要。
open: The thing I would name is not a tool, it is a rule I made about when I am allowed to use them, and it has done more for me than any of the tools themselves.
我要说的不是某个工具，而是我给自己定的一条关于“什么时候才允许用它们”的规矩；它对我的作用，比那些工具本身加起来都大。

The reason is that everything in this area is designed by people whose job is to make it difficult to stop, and treating that as a contest of willpower is a losing position. I lost it repeatedly for about a decade. What works is not resisting in the moment but removing the moment — changing where a thing lives so that using it takes one deliberate step instead of none, because a single deliberate step is enough to break an automatic reach.
原因是，这个领域里的一切，都是由一群以“让你难以停下来”为职业的人设计的；把这当成一场意志力的较量，是一个必输的位置。我在这上面反复输了大概十年。真正有用的，不是在当下抵抗，而是把那个“当下”拿掉——改变一样东西存放的位置，让使用它需要一个刻意的动作，而不是零个动作；因为哪怕只有一个刻意的动作，也足以打断一次自动的伸手。

The concrete version is that nothing I want to use less lives on the first screen of my phone, and two things live only on a laptop I have to physically go and open. That is the whole system. It sounds trivial and the effect was not: within about six weeks my usage of the things I had moved dropped by something like two thirds, and I did not resist anything or feel deprived at any point, because the reaching had simply stopped happening.
具体的版本是：所有我希望少用的东西，都不放在手机的第一屏；有两样只存在于一台我必须走过去打开的笔记本上。整个系统就这么多。听起来微不足道，效果并不是：大概六个星期之内，我对那些被挪走的东西的使用量降了差不多三分之二，而我全程没有抵抗过任何东西，也没有感到被剥夺，因为那个“伸手”本身就不再发生了。
So my answer is that I no longer try to have better habits here. I try to make the bad ones slightly inconvenient, which turns out to be a far more reliable mechanism than intending to do better.
所以我的答案是：我不再试图在这方面养成更好的习惯，我只是让坏习惯稍微不方便一点。而这被证明是一个比“打算做得更好”可靠得多的机制。
What I would say is slow and in one place, and if you had asked me at twenty-five I would have described five cities in ten days and meant it.
我会说：慢一点，而且待在一个地方。如果你在我二十五岁时问，我会给你描述十天五座城市，而且是认真的。

The reason I changed is noticing that almost nothing good happens on the second day somewhere. The second day is admin — finding the shop, working out the transport, discovering which place is actually good rather than merely nearest. If you leave on the third morning you have paid all of that cost and collected none of the return. Staying put means you get the version of a place that only exists once you have stopped being a visitor to it.
我改变的原因，是我发现到了一个地方的第二天几乎不会发生什么好事。第二天全是杂事——找超市、研究交通、弄清楚哪家店是真的好而不只是最近。如果第三天早上就走，你把这些成本都付了，却一点回报都没拿到。待着不动，你才能看到一个地方在你不再是“游客”之后的样子。

The trip that proved it was two summers ago. We rented a flat in one small town for ten days and did almost nothing that would look good written down. Same café every morning — by the fourth day the woman behind the counter had our order ready — same beach, and twice we did not leave the flat until noon. On the last evening a neighbour we had said hello to all week invited us in for a drink, which would never have happened on day two.
证明这一点的是前年夏天那次。我们在一个小城租了十天的公寓，做的事情几乎没有一件写下来好看的。每天早上去同一家咖啡馆——到第四天，柜台后面那位女士已经提前把我们要的准备好了；同一片海滩；有两天我们中午之前根本没出门。最后一天晚上，一个我们打了一星期招呼的邻居请我们进去喝了一杯，这种事在第二天是绝不可能发生的。
So the way I judge a trip now is almost embarrassingly simple: how many times did I open and close the suitcase? One is ideal. Anything above three and I have booked a trip rather than a rest.
所以我现在判断一次旅行好不好的标准简单得有点不好意思：我一共开合了几次行李箱？一次最理想。超过三次，我订的就是一次行程，而不是一次休息。
The part I would keep, if I could only keep one, is the problem-solving — and I would say that regardless of what the job has been called, which is the reason I trust it as an answer.
如果只能保留一样，我会保留解决问题的过程。而且不管这份工作叫什么名字，我都会这么说，这也是我信任这个答案的原因。

The reason it holds is that I need to be able to point at something at the end of a day and say it is different because I was there. A great deal of professional work does not pass that test. You attend, you contribute, you go home, and if you had been ill that day the outcome would have been broadly the same. That is not a complaint about anybody — coordination work is genuinely shaped that way — but it means the days I feel good about are the ones where something was broken at nine and was not by five.
它之所以成立，是因为我需要在一天结束时，能指着某样东西说：这里因为我而不同。相当多的职业工作过不了这一关。你出席、你发言、你回家；如果那天你请病假，结果大概也差不多。这不是在抱怨谁——协调性的工作本来就是这个形状——但这意味着，让我觉得好的日子，是那种“九点有东西坏着、五点不坏了”的日子。

The clearest recent case was a report my team produced every week that took about three hours because two systems disagreed about how to name things. Everybody complained and nobody fixed it, for the ordinary reason that fixing it was not anybody's job. I spent two days on it and it now takes ten minutes. Nine people got two and a half hours of their week back, permanently. That felt better than the promotion I had the year before, and I have thought about why ever since.
最近最清楚的一次，是我们组每周都要出的一份报告，要花大概三个小时，因为两个系统对同一样东西的命名方式不一致。所有人都抱怨，但没有人去修，理由很平常：修它不是任何人的职责。我花了两天，现在十分钟就能出。九个人从此每周永久多出两个半小时。那种感觉比我前一年升职还好，而我从那以后一直在想为什么。
So what keeps me in a role is not where it leads. It is whether the work has that shape — a before, an after, and my hand visible in the difference.
所以让我留在一个岗位上的，不是它通向哪里，而是这份工作有没有那个形状：有一个之前，有一个之后，而我的手在那个差别里看得见。
yesno: Yes, though I would have said no for most of my twenties, and what changed was not the work but what I was measuring it against.
是的，不过我二十多岁的大部分时间会说不是；而改变的不是工作，是我拿什么在衡量它。

The reason is that I used to judge a job by whether it was the right job, as though there were a correct one somewhere and my task was to find it. That framing makes every role feel provisional, because there is always something you have not tried. At some point I swapped it for a much duller question — is this week better than most weeks I could realistically be having — and almost everything became easier to answer, including this.
原因是，我以前判断一份工作，看的是它是不是“对的那份”，好像某个地方存在一个正确答案，而我的任务是找到它。这个框架会让每一个岗位都显得是临时的，因为总有你还没试过的东西。到某个时候我把它换成了一个乏味得多的问题——这一周，比我现实中可能过的大多数星期更好吗——之后几乎所有事情都变得容易回答了，包括这一件。

The moment it shifted was a conversation with somebody about ten years older who asked what I would do differently if I accepted that no job was going to be the right one. I did not have an answer ready. Thinking about it afterwards, the honest reply was that I would stop treating everything as a step towards something and start noticing whether I liked Tuesday. I made two fairly small changes off the back of that — what I said yes to, and when I stopped in the evening — and the job I already had improved considerably without changing at all.
转折点是和一个比我大十岁左右的人的一次谈话。他问我：如果你接受了没有哪份工作会是“对的那份”，你会有什么不同的做法？我当时没有现成的答案。事后想明白，诚实的回答是：我会不再把一切都当成通往某处的台阶，而开始注意自己喜不喜欢星期二。基于这个我做了两个不大的改动——我答应什么，以及晚上几点停下来——结果我手上那份一点没变的工作，明显变好了。
So the answer is yes, and I am fairly sure it is a yes about how I am approaching it rather than about the work itself.
所以答案是肯定的，而且我相当确定，这个“是”是关于我怎么对待它的，而不是关于工作本身。
